inline.s: Course
Textbook
Written by National Master Bojo Chinul of Goryeo
Seek not the Buddha far on Vulture Peak; / The Vulture Peak is in your mind to seek.
Each person has a Vulture Peak tower; / There cultivate, hour by hour.
Recognize the dharmakaya, not the physical body;
Recognize the numinous knowing, not deluded thoughts.
One who awakens to this and guards it sits in the single suchness and attains unmoving liberation;
One who is deluded and turns from it drifts through the six realms and circles through long eons.
[The Vulture Peak is right in your mind]
The Sixth Patriarch said:

'The physical body of the ordinary person is a city; the eyes, ears, nose, and tongue are its gates. Outside there are five gates, and within there is the mind-gate. The mind is the ground and the nature is the king; the king dwells upon the ground of the mind. When the nature is present, the king is present; when the nature departs, the king is gone. When the nature is present, body and mind survive; when the nature departs, body and mind are destroyed. The Buddha is realized within the nature; do not seek him outside the body. When the self-nature is deluded, that is the sentient being; when the self-nature is awakened, that is the Buddha.'
(see
Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch
The Flower Garland Sutra
Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathagata says:
'There is not one sentient being that does not fully possess the Tathagata's wisdom; but because of false thinking and inverted attachments, they fail to realize it;
if they abandon false thinking
, then the wisdom of all things, the natural wisdom, and the unobstructed wisdom all become manifest now.'
if one abandons false thinking

There are three levels here: the coarse thought ceases, the subtle thought ceases, and then even the extremely subtle thought ceases. For example, for a reciter of the Buddha's name, false thoughts are the coarse thought, while the thought of reciting the Buddha's name is the subtle thought. Ordinarily, when both coarse and subtle thoughts have subsided, this is called no-thought; this is no-thought as generally spoken of. Going further, if even the extremely subtle thought also stops, this is the ultimate no-thought. Therefore, the meaning of the term no-thought must be determined according to its context. [Extremely subtle thought] The extremely subtle arising and ceasing and flowing of the cognitive mind is an aspect of the alayavijnana (store consciousness). The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
'When the bodhisattva's stage is exhausted
(having fully fulfilled the ten stages)
, satisfying the expedient means, in a single thought corresponding, the mind of awakening first arises, and the mind has no initial aspect;
because of being apart from extremely subtle thought,
one sees the mind-nature,
and the mind is then ever-abiding,
which is called ultimate awakening
Master Guifeng said:
'If the extremely subtle flowing stream
(the extremely subtle thought)

is entirely stilled, only the great wisdom of perfect awakening stands alone, bright and clear; then according with circumstances it manifests hundreds of billions of bodies to save sentient beings of karmic connection,
and this is called being a Buddha
(See the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp of the Jingde Era.)

[Wisdom of all things] Of all inner dharmas and inner names, it can know and understand; of all outer dharmas and outer names, it too can know and understand. [Natural wisdom] The wisdom that arises of itself, with no reliance on applied effort. [Unobstructed wisdom] The wisdom that is freely unobstructed, that is, the Buddha's wisdom.
The Surangama Sutra says:
'All sentient beings, from beginningsless time, in the continuity of birth and death, all because they do not know the ever-abiding true mind as the pure and bright essence of the nature,
(that is, because they do not know that their abiding in the true mind is this pure and bright essence of the nature)
, they employ a multitude of false thoughts
(and because they employ false thoughts)
; these thoughts are not true, and therefore there is transmigration.'

[True mind as pure and bright essence of nature] Pure and bright essence of nature is the bright, wondrous essence whose nature is originally pure. From the grammatical structure, pure and bright essence of nature is an appositive, used to modify the noun true mind. [Transmigration] The birth-and-death of delimited divisions and the birth-and-death of transformation. [Birth-and-death of delimited divisions] Among sentient beings in the three realms and six paths, because of what their wholesome and unwholesome karma produces, their lifespans all have limits and their physical forms all have separate sections; hence their birth-and-death is called birth-and-death of delimited divisions. One who is liberated from birth-and-death of delimited divisions escapes the wheel of transmigration. [Birth-and-death of transformation] The noble ones of the three vehicles, having already cut off the delusions of views and attachment and transcended the birth-and-death of delimited divisions, in the course of cultivation their deluded thoughts gradually cease and their realization gradually grows. This transition from delusion to awakening differs in each stage; as one moves from an earlier stage to a later one, it is just like one death and rebirth, and its transformation is so subtle and unfathomable that it is inconceivable; hence it is called birth-and-death of transformation. One who is liberated from the birth-and-death of transformation fully realizes Buddhahood.
Master Guifeng said:

'All dharmas are like a dream, as all the noble ones alike declare. Therefore false thoughts are originally still, and the realms of dust are originally empty. The empty, still mind is numinous knowing, never dimmed.
This very empty and still knowing is your true nature.

. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind is originally self-aware; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it arise because of objects. This single word knowing is the gate to all wonders. Because of delusion from beginnings, we falsely grasp body and mind as self and give rise to thoughts of greed and hatred. If one obtains the guidance of a good friend and suddenly awakens to this empty, still knowing, this knowing is without thought and without form, then who is the sign of self and the sign of person? Awakening that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately awaken; when awakened, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here. Thus, though one may perfectly cultivate myriad practices, one takes no-thought as the sole essence. Once one has the view of no-thought, then love and aversion naturally become faint, compassion and wisdom naturally grow bright, karmic offenses naturally cease, and meritorious practice naturally advances. Having understood that all marks are no-mark, there is naturally the cultivation of no-cultivation. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are extinguished. When arising and ceasing have ceased, still illumination appears before one, applied without end; this is called being Buddha.'
(From the Preface to the Collection of the Various Commentaries on the Sources of Chan.)
empty, still knowing

also called numinous knowing. [Awakening that all marks are empty, the mind is naturally without thought. When a thought arises, immediately awaken; when awakened, it is gone. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies precisely here.] Awakening that all marks are illusory, the mind is naturally without thought. If a false thought arises, one must immediately awaken to the fact that one is taking illusion to be real and being turned by illusory marks. Once one awakens to this, the false thought immediately vanishes. The wondrous gate of cultivation lies right here!

inline.s: A brief introduction to National Master Bojo:
Chinul (
, roughly the Southern Song period in China), also written Zhinu (
ne

), the founding patriarch of the Korean Jogye Order. A native of Dongju in Gyeongseo (Seoheung County, Hwanghae Province), he went by the style name the Oxherder. His lay surname was Zheng. At the age of eight he left home under Priest Jonghwi of Jogyesan. After receiving the full precepts, he formed a society with more than ten fellow students to practice concentration and wisdom. At twenty-five he passed the monastic examination and resided at Cheongwon Temple in Changpyeong, where he had an awakening through reading the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch. At twenty-eight he moved to Pumun Temple at Hagasan, where he obtained Li Tongxuan's Commentary on the Avatamsaka Sutra (the New Avatamsaka Commentary) of the Tang dynasty, and realized that the essential teaching of Chan accords with the doctrine of the Avatamsaka. Later, at Geojosa temple on Palgongsan, he composed the Cultivation of Concentration and Wisdom Society Letter to spur himself on in actual practice. After several years he retired to Muju Hermitage on Jirisan, devoted entirely to inner contemplation. One day, reading the Record of Dahui, he suddenly had a great awakening. In the third year of the reign of King Sinjong (

), he again formed a society at Gilseong Temple on Songgwangsan, and over some eleven years devoted himself to spreading Jogye Chan, advocating immediate awakening followed by gradual cultivation, and the equal maintenance of concentration and wisdom. Afterward he founded the White Cloud Retreat on Ibosang, the Jipseok Hermitage, the Joyang Hermitage, and others. In the first year of King Huijong (
), he changed Jeonghye Temple on Songgwangsan into the Jogyesan Cultivation Society, which became the fundamental center of Korean Zen.
In the sixth year of King Huijong (

), in spring, the master knew the time of his passing had come. On the night before his nirvana, while he was bathing, an attendant kept asking him questions; the master answered each one calmly. At dawn the next day (on the twenty-seventh day of the third month), everyone came to see him off. The master had the attendant strike the drum to gather the assembly, and, staff in hand, he strode briskly into the Dharma hall, ascended the seat, and gave a lecture. He said: 'The efficacy of Chan is inconceivable. Today, having come here, I intend to set forth clearly this inconceivable mystery for you. Whoever wishes may now come up and ask; I, this old man, will surely answer you one by one.' Everyone began to ask questions, and the master responded according to each, with unobstructed eloquence. Having answered the final question, he tapped his staff on the ground several times and said: 'Say a thousand words, say ten thousand words, all of it is right here.' Having spoken, he sat serenely and passed away tranquilly.

The master lived to fifty-three, with a Dharma age of thirty-six; his posthumous title was National Master Buddha-Sun Bojo. He authored the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, the Cultivation of Mind Essentials, the Essential Selections from the Separate Transmission Record of the Dharma Collection with Personal Notes, the Treatise on the Perfect and Sudden Attainment of Buddhahood, the Treatise on Resolving Doubt in the Hua-tou, the Essential Gate of Buddha-Recitation, the Postscript to the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and others. His Dharma heirs included Huichen, Zhengxuan, Shouyu, and others.

[Full precepts] The complete and perfect precepts, such as the two hundred and fifty precepts of a monk and the three hundred and forty-eight precepts of a nun. [Monastic examination] The examination system for monastics implemented in Korea from the Goryeo period to the early Joseon dynasty. It was divided into the sectarian examination and the great examination. The sectarian examination was administered by the temples, while the great examination was administered by the state. Only those who passed the sectarian examination could take the great examination. The great examination was divided into a Chan-sect great examination and a doctrinal-sect great examination; the former was held at Gwangmyeong Temple, the chief temple of the Chan school, and the latter at Wangnyun Temple, the chief temple of the doctrinal school. The great examination was held once every three years. [Li Tongxuan (

)] Known in the world as Venerable Li, and also called the Great Adept of Jujube and Cypress, he was a Avatamsaka scholar of the Tang dynasty, a native of Cangzhou (present-day southeast of Cangxian, Hebei). In his youth he studied the principles of the Book of Changes; after the age of about forty he devoted himself to Buddhist scriptures, focusing deeply on the Avatamsaka Sutra. At that time the eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka had just been translated. In the spring of the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era (

), he carried the newly translated Avatamsaka Sutra to the home of Gao Shannu in Daxian Village, Tongying Township, southwest of Meng County in Taiyuan, and there composed a treatise to clarify the meaning of the scripture. For three years he never left the house; it is said that each day he ate only ten jujubes and one cypress-leaf cake in the morning, and so the world called him the Great Adept of Jujube and Cypress. He later carried his draft to an earthen shrine at the foot of Shenfushan (the earthen shrine at Fangshan, Shouyang, Taiyuan) to continue his writing, and after five years it was completed; this is the forty-fascicle New Avatamsaka Commentary. He then also wrote the four-fascicle Brief Explanation of the New Avatamsaka Sutra's Stages of Cultivation and Resolving Doubt. In the eighteenth year of the Kaiyuan era (
), though some say the twenty-eighth year of the Kaiyuan era (

), on the twenty-eighth day of the third month, he passed into nirvana at the age of ninety-six. [Avatamsaka Sutra] Its full title is the Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra of the Buddha, a central scripture in which, after his enlightenment at the Bodhimanda and elsewhere, the Buddha, by means of the great bodhisattvas Samantabhadra and Manjushri, reveals the causal practice and resultant virtue of the Tathagata. This scripture has three Chinese translations: First, the translation by Buddhabhadra of the Eastern Jin, titled Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, in sixty fascicles; to distinguish it from the later Tang translation it is called the old translation of the Avatamsaka, or the sixty-fascicle Avatamsaka. Second, the translation by Shikshananda of the Tang era of Empress Wu Zetian, titled Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, in eighty fascicles, also called the new translation of the Avatamsaka, or the eighty-fascicle Avatamsaka. Third, the translation by Prajna in the Zhenyuan era of the Tang, also titled Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, in forty fascicles; its full title is the Great Vaipulya Avatamsaka Sutra, the Conduct and Vows of Samantabhadra's Entry into the Inconceivable Realm of Liberation, abbreviated as the Conduct and Vows of Samantabhadra, or the forty-fascicle Avatamsaka.

blocks.text: Title Explanation

inline.s: [Direct Explanation of the True Mind]
In this essay, the true mind is what is generally called the self-nature. Direct explanation means speaking as it truly is, stating it plainly and straightforwardly.

The Direct Explanation of the True Mind treats the true mind (the self-nature) comprehensively from the following fifteen aspects: Right Faith in the True Mind, the Different Names of the True Mind, the Wondrous Essence of the True Mind, the Wondrous Function of the True Mind, Oneness and Difference of Essence and Function, the True Mind in Delusion, Pacifying False Thoughts of the True Mind, the Four Deportments of the True Mind, Where the True Mind Abides, the True Mind Beyond Death, the Principal and Auxiliary Practices, the Merits of the True Mind, Verifying the Merit of the True Mind, the True Mind Without Knowing, and Where the True Mind Goes. It illuminates the true mind (the self-nature) originally possessed by everyone, the root of delusion and awakening, and the path of cultivation and the realms of realization.
The Direct Explanation of the True Mind is a companion piece to the Cultivation of Mind Essentials (see
Annotated Cultivation of Mind Essentials

The self-nature is the essence, and the mind is the function of the self-nature. The mind has two states: the original mind and the cognitive mind. The original mind is the original state of the mind, luminous, clear, and profoundly translucent, standing alone and independent. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

'If you do not recognize the original mind, studying the Dharma is of no benefit. If you recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature, then you are called a great man, teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha.'
The cognitive mind is also called the
thought-discriminating mind

— the mind that arises by clinging to and discriminating the six objects of sense, which is what the Buddha calls the shadow cast by conditions of the six senses in the Sutra of Perfect Awakening. It is the mind that is present in our daily use, discriminating and knowing, that is, the thought of the present moment. Its characteristic is discrimination and calculation, delighting in one and rejecting the other. The arising of a thought, seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing (the knowing here is the discriminating knowing) — these are all the working of the cognitive mind.
The original mind is undefiled, so it is also called the mind of pure self-nature. The original mind is without knowing yet knows everything, so the original mind is also called the
mind of numinous knowing

. It should be noted: the knowing of numinous knowing is the knowing of non-knowing; to distinguish it from the mark-grasping knowing of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, it is called numinous knowing. The Record of the Mirror of the School says:
'Prajna is without knowing — it has no knowing that grasps marks.'
The Surangama Sutra says:
'To establish knowing upon views is the root of ignorance; when views no longer see, this is nirvana, the undefiled true purity.'
Cultivation is to still this scattered cognitive mind (the thought-discriminating mind) and thereby reach the state of the original mind (the mind of numinous knowing), as it is said:
'When the wild mind is not stilled, still it; when stilled, this is bodhi.'
. The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says:
'Still thought and forget
(let go of)
deliberation, and the Buddha himself appears before you.'
The Treasury of the Buddha-dharma Sutra says:
'The anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas is without thinking and without thought.'

Cultivation is to return to the source, to transform the state of the cognitive mind (the mind that discriminates by clinging to the six sense objects) into the state of the original mind (the empty, still, numinously knowing mind). To awaken is to awaken to this empty, still, numinously knowing mind; to cultivate is to guard this empty, still, numinously knowing mind. First protect, then let go, until reaching non-activity.
It should be noted, however, that in general discussions the essence and function, and the delusion and awakening, of the substance are often given separate names. For instance, the essay
Mind, Self-Nature, and the Tathagata-garbha

, for the sake of convenience in discussion, gives separate names to the essence and function and to delusion and awakening of the substance: the self-nature is the essence, and the mind is its function. The state of the self-nature's awakening is called the original nature (the tathagata-garbha, the Buddha-nature); the state of the self-nature's delusion is called the cognitive nature (the store of cognition). The state of the mind's awakening is called the original mind (the true mind); the state of the mind's delusion is called the cognitive mind (the deluded mind). In the Direct Explanation of the True Mind, however, apart from an occasional use of the term deluded mind, it ordinarily uses only the term true mind, not distinguishing essence from function and using it for both delusion and awakening. On this point, chapter two, The Different Names of the True Mind, discriminates very clearly, and states:

'If one penetrates the true mind, all names are understood; if one is benighted about the true mind, all names are obstructed. Therefore, with regard to the true mind, one should look into it with care.'
Thus, whether the true mind in a given sentence refers to essence or function, delusion or awakening, should be discerned according to the context.
A note:
In the annotations, for ease of reading and understanding, when the quoted original text is rendered into plain language, quotation marks are likewise added. For example, the original text:
The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.'

And the annotated rendering: The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path, the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.' Therefore, the text within quotation marks in the annotations is not necessarily the original; readers are asked to note this.

blocks.text: 1. Right Faith in the True Mind

inline.s: [The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.' Again, the Consciousness-Only treatises say: 'Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can purify muddy water.' Thus, when all good things arise, faith leads the way. That is why Buddhist scriptures set 'Thus have I heard' at the beginning; this is what is meant by giving rise to faith.]

The Avatamsaka Sutra says: 'Faith is the source of the path, the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.' Again, the Treatise on the Perfection of Consciousness Only says: 'Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can clarify muddy water.' Thus we know that when all good things arise, faith leads the way. That is why all Buddhist scriptures open with 'Thus have I heard' — precisely to lead readers to give rise to faith in the scriptures.
[Faith] To believe and to delight in. The faith in this passage refers to faith in the correct Dharma, and so it says:
'Faith is the source of the path and the mother of merit, nurturing all roots of goodness.'
It also says:
'Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can purify muddy water.'

[Roots of goodness] The good of the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, firm and unremovable, is called root. Again, good can produce wondrous fruits and give rise to further good, hence it is called root. [Faith is like the clear-water jewel, because it can purify muddy water] Faith in the correct Dharma is like the clear-water jewel that can clarify muddy water, able to purify the confused, deluded mind. [Clear-water jewel] As the saying goes: In the Western regions there is a treasure called the clear-water jewel. When this jewel is cast into muddy water, for every inch it enters, one inch of the muddy water becomes clear. As the jewel descends from inch to foot and to the bottom, all the muddy water accordingly becomes clear. [Thus have I heard] This is what I (Ānanda) personally heard and saw (not what was passed on by hearsay). 'Thus have I heard' is a means of establishing trust, proving that this scripture is indeed spoken by the Buddha and that the recorded text is correct and without error. The 'I' in the phrase is the self-designation of Ānanda, the compiler of the scripture. Ānanda was the Buddha's cousin, born on the night of the Buddha's enlightenment. Later he left home under the Buddha and served as his attendant, being renowned for never forgetting what he heard, foremost in extensive learning. When Ānanda left home, the Buddha had already taught for twenty years, so he asked the Buddha to repeat to him all that had been spoken before; at the same time, Ānanda also attained the samadhi of the Self-Awakened Dharma-Nature, whereby he could fully penetrate all dharmas in concentration. Thus, after the Buddha's nirvana, when the Venerable Mahakashyapa assembled the canon at the Great Stone Cavern in the kingdom of Magadha, five hundred great arhats gathered together, and the assembly unanimously asked Ānanda to ascend the seat and recite the scriptures.

[Someone asked: What difference is there between the faith of the ancestral school and the faith of the doctrinal school? Reply: There are several differences. The doctrinal school leads gods and men to have faith in cause and effect: those who love blessings and pleasures are taught to believe that the ten wholesome deeds are the wondrous cause and the realm of gods and men the pleasing fruit; those who delight in emptiness and stillness are taught to believe that the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing are the correct cause and the four noble truths (suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path) the noble fruit; those who delight in the fruit of Buddhahood are taught to believe that the six perfections over three incalculable eons are the great cause and the attainment of bodhi and nirvana the correct fruit.]

Question: What difference is there between the faith of the ancestral school (the patriarch school, Chan) and the faith of the doctrinal school (the text-based school)? Reply: There are several differences. The doctrinal school causes sentient beings in the human and heavenly realms to have faith in cause and effect: for those who love to enjoy blessings and pleasures, it tells them to believe that the ten wholesome deeds are the wondrous cause of blessings and pleasures, and birth as a human or god is the pleasing fruit; for those who delight in emptiness and stillness, it tells them to believe that the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing are the correct cause of emptiness and stillness, and the realization of the four noble truths (suffering, its arising, its cessation, and the path) is the noble fruit; for those who delight in the fruit of Buddhahood, it tells them to believe that the wondrous practices of the six perfections over three incalculable eons are the great cause of becoming a Buddha, and the realization of bodhi and nirvana is the correct fruit.

[Doctrinal school] One that takes the scriptural teachings as the gate to the path. The Chan school calls itself the ancestral school (entering the path by the patriarchs' mind-to-mind transmission) and commonly calls other schools the doctrinal schools. [Four noble truths] The truth of suffering, the truth of its arising, the truth of its cessation, and the truth of the path. First, the truth of suffering explains the truth that life is full of suffering. Suffering has the characteristic of oppression. Life has the three sufferings, the eight sufferings, and immeasurable sufferings; suffering is the true reality of actual life. Second, the arising in the truth of arising means to bring about, to cause; it explains the truth of how the suffering of life comes about. The suffering of life comes from clinging and craving that create karma, and so one undergoes suffering and transmigration. Third, the truth of cessation explains the truth of extinguishing all suffering. When all the arising of suffering (craving) is forever cut off without remainder, undefiled and unattached, one no longer undergoes suffering and transmigration; this is the truth of cessation. Fourth, the truth of the path explains how to forever cut off the arising of suffering (craving), that is, the path that extinguishes suffering — the noble eightfold path. Among the four noble truths, arising is the cause and suffering the fruit; the path is the cause and cessation the fruit. [Three sufferings] The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioned existence. The suffering of suffering: worldly people already have a body subject to birth and death, which is suffering enough; added to this the oppression of many sufferings is truly suffering upon suffering, hence it is called the suffering of suffering. The suffering of decay is the suffering felt when a happiness that briefly appears is lost. The suffering of conditioned existence is the suffering of all conditioned things being impermanent, flowing on without rest and never settling. [Eight sufferings] First, the suffering of birth, the pain at the time of birth; second, the suffering of old age, the pain of age and weakness; third, the suffering of illness, the pain of being sick; fourth, the suffering of death, the pain at the time of death; fifth, the suffering of separation from what one loves, the pain of parting from those one loves; sixth, the suffering of meeting what one hates, the pain of meeting those one despises; seventh, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, the pain of not getting what one wishes; eighth, the suffering of the blazing of the five aggregates, that is, the fierce activity of the five aggregates covering the true nature.

[Noble eightfold path] Also called the eightfold correct path, the eight practices of the noble ones: first, right view, that is, correct understanding and vision; second, right thought, that is, correct reflection; third, right speech, that is, proper words; fourth, right action, that is, proper conduct; fifth, right livelihood, that is, a proper occupation and way of life; sixth, right effort, that is, correct striving; seventh, right mindfulness, that is, correct awareness; eighth, right concentration, that is, correct meditation. Cultivating this noble eightfold path, one can realize the fruit of arhatship. [Three incalculable eons] This is the time it takes a bodhisattva to cultivate to Buddhahood. The asankhyeya eon is translated in Chinese as countless long time. The stages by which a bodhisattva cultivates up to Buddhahood total fifty. Of these: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications, forty stages in all, constitute the first incalculable eon; among the ten grounds, from the first ground to the seventh ground is the second incalculable eon; from the eighth ground to the tenth ground is the third incalculable eon. After the tenth ground one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.

[The right faith of the ancestral school is not the same as the above. It does not believe in the cause and effect of all conditioned things; it merely requires believing that one is originally a Buddha: the true and spontaneous self-nature is fully possessed by everyone, and the wondrous essence of nirvana is perfected in each; one does not rely on seeking it elsewhere, for it has been complete all along. The Third Patriarch says: 'Round like the great void, lacking nothing and having nothing over; it is all because of grasping and rejecting, and so it is not thus.' Master Zhi says: 'Within the marked body there is the unmarked body; upon the road of ignorance there is the road of no-birth.' Yongjia says: 'The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya.' Therefore know that sentient beings are originally Buddha.]

The right faith of the ancestral school is not the same as the faith of the doctrinal school described above. The ancestral school does not believe in the cause and effect of all conditioned dharmas; it merely requires believing that one is originally a Buddha: the true and spontaneous self-nature is fully possessed by everyone, and the wondrous essence of nirvana is perfected in each; one does not rely on seeking it elsewhere, for it has been complete all along. The Third Patriarch of the Chan school, Sengcan, says: 'The true and spontaneous self-nature, round like the great void, lacking nothing and having nothing over — it is all on account of a mind of grasping and rejecting that the original nature does not appear (is not thus).' The Venerable Baozhi says: 'Within the marked body (the physical body) there is the unmarked body (the true mind); upon the road of ignorance there is the road of no-birth (the road of nirvana).' The Song of Realizing the Way by Master Yongjia says: 'The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya.' Therefore know that sentient beings are originally Buddha.

[Cause and effect of conditioned things] The cause and effect of conditioned dharmas. [Conditioned dharmas] All things that arise from the combination of causes and conditions. [Thusness] The true, unchanging nature of all things. This nature is extremely difficult to describe in words, and so the character 'thus' is used to represent it. The original nature is the real mark; the real mark is thusness, because it is non-dual, unchanging, immutable, and unmoving; the true face of all dharmas is the same single mark, and so it is called 'thus.' [Real mark] The true state of dharmas. 'The real mark of all dharmas' is the true state of all dharmas. In the

Buddha-Recitation Chapter, the second, of the Treasury of the Buddha-dharma Sutra, the Buddha says: 'What is called the real mark of all dharmas? That is to say, all dharmas are ultimately empty, without any being.' (For a detailed discussion of the real mark of all dharmas, see
The Real Mark of All Dharmas

one essay.) [The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya] This means: ignorance arises from the Buddha-nature (the true mind in delusion), and the physical body is a manifestation of the dharmakaya.

The Essential Methods of the Transmission of Mind says: 'This one mind alone is the Buddha, and the Buddha and sentient beings are no different. But because sentient beings cling to marks and seek without, they lose it the more they seek; making the Buddha seek the Buddha, using the mind to grasp the mind, throughout eons and the whole of their lives they can never attain it. They do not know that when they still thought and forget (let go of) deliberation, the Buddha himself appears before them. This mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is the sentient being. When one is a sentient being, this mind is not diminished; when one is a Buddha, this mind is not increased. Indeed, the six perfections and myriad practices and the merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are originally complete in themselves, not depending on cultivation or addition; when conditions arise they are given forth, and when conditions cease they are still. If one is not resolved, and does not believe that this is the Buddha, but wishes to cultivate by clinging to marks to seek meritorious function, all of it is false thinking and runs counter to the path. This mind is the Buddha; there is no other Buddha, and no other mind. This mind is bright and pure, like empty space, with not a single mark. The moment one raises a thought, one departs from the essence of Dharma and clings to a mark; since beginnings there has never been a Buddha who clings to marks. To cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices seeking to become a Buddha is itself a ladder of stages; since beginnings there has never been a Buddha attained by stages.'

It also says: 'Apart from all marks, sentient beings and all Buddhas are not at all different; only when one can be without mind is that the ultimate. A student of the path, if he is not immediately without mind, though he cultivate through many eons will never accomplish the path, being bound by the practices of the three vehicles and unable to gain liberation. Yet the realization of this mind may be quick or slow. There are those who, on hearing the Dharma in a single thought, become without mind; there are those who reach it only at the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, and the ten dedications; and there are those who reach it only at the ten grounds. Whether it takes long or short, it is only upon becoming without mind that one abides; then there is nothing more to cultivate or realize. In truth there is nothing attained; this is real and not false. To attain it in a single thought and to attain it at the tenth ground are exactly the same in function, with no further depth or shallowness; it is only that through the eons one labors in vain.'

[Fifty-two stages] In going from an ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva passes through fifty-two stages in all: the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten dedications, the ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment.
Q: The Chan school often says, '
See the mind and realize the nature,
and realizing the nature, become a Buddha.' What does this mean?
Answer:
See the mind and realize the nature
' means:

recognize your own original mind and see your own original nature. 'And realizing the nature, become a Buddha' means: having seen your own original nature, then cultivate in accord with the nature and perfectly fulfill the Buddha way.

Thus, 'see the mind and realize the nature, and realizing the nature become a Buddha' means: recognize your own original mind, see your own original nature, then cultivate in accord with the nature and perfectly fulfill the Buddha way. (See
Annotated Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch

[Once right faith is born, it must be nourished with understanding. Yongming says: 'Faith without understanding increases ignorance; understanding without faith increases wrong views.' Therefore know that when faith and understanding are combined, one quickly enters the path.]

Once right faith is born, it must be nourished by understanding. Master Yongming says: 'Faith without understanding increases ignorance; understanding without faith increases wrong views.' Therefore know that when faith and understanding are combined, one can quickly enter the path (see the mind and realize the nature).

[Entering the path] Seeing the mind and realizing the nature. So far as the Chan school is concerned, before entering the path is the preliminary practice; after entering the path (sudden awakening) is the practice of cultivation (gradual cultivation); and after that is the realization of the path. The realm of realizing the path is as described in Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way. The Consciousness-Only school has a doctrine of five stages of cultivation: the stage of the equipment of merits, the stage of applied practice, the stage of clear penetration, the stage of cultivation, and the stage of ultimate attainment.

[Someone asked: If one has just given rise to the resolve of faith and has not yet entered the path, is there any benefit? Reply: The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: 'If a person, having heard this Dharma, gives rise to no timidity or weakness, know that such a person will certainly succeed to the Buddha-seed and will certainly be given the prophecy by all Buddhas. Even if a person could transform all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm and lead them to practice the ten wholesome deeds, it would not compare with a person who, in a single moment of thought, rightly ponders this Dharma; the merit of the latter surpasses the former beyond all comparison.' Again, the Prajna Sutra says: 'Those who, even in a single thought, give rise to pure faith, the Tathagata knows and sees them all; these sentient beings obtain such immeasurable blessings.']

Question: If one has just given rise to the resolve of faith (believing that one is originally a Buddha) and has not yet realized and entered the noble path, is there any benefit? Reply: The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: 'If a person, having heard this Dharma (that one is originally a Buddha), gives rise to no timidity or weakness, know that such a person is certainly a seed of Buddhahood and will certainly receive the prophecy from all Buddhas. Even if a person could deliver all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm and lead them to practice the ten wholesome deeds, it would not match a person who, in a single moment of thought, rightly ponders this Dharma (that one is originally a Buddha); the merit of the latter far exceeds the former and cannot be described.' Again, the Diamond Sutra (Vajracchedika Prajna Paramita Sutra) says: 'Those who, even in a single thought, give rise to pure faith, the Tathagata fully knows and sees them; these sentient beings obtain such immeasurable blessings.'
[Vyakarana] The Buddha names in advance (records the name): after how many ages, in such and such a place, in such and such a land, one will become what Buddha.

[Thus know: to walk a thousand miles, the first step must be right; if the first step is wrong, the whole thousand miles are wrong. To enter the land of the unconditioned, the initial faith must be right; once the initial faith is lost, all good retreats. Therefore the patriarch said: “A hairsbreadth’s deviation, and heaven and earth are set apart.” This is the principle.]

Therefore know: to walk a thousand miles, the first step must be right; if the first step is wrong, then all the thousand miles that follow are wholly wrong. To enter the land of the unconditioned (the true mind), the initial faith must be right (one must believe that one is originally a Buddha); if the initial faith is lost and not right, then all good retreats. Therefore the patriarch said: “A hairsbreadth’s deviation, and heaven and earth are set apart.” This is the principle.
[The unconditioned] That which is made by no causes or conditions. [The land of the unconditioned] Another name for the true mind (see the next chapter, “The True Mind’s Other Names”).

blocks.text: 2. The True Mind’s Other Names

inline.s: [Someone says: I have already given rise to right faith, but I do not know what is named the true mind. The answer: Apart from delusion it is called true; numinous awareness is called mind. The Surangama Sutra sets forth and reveals this mind.]

Someone asks: I have already given rise to right faith, but I do not know what is called the true mind. The answer: Apart from delusion it is called true; numinous knowing is called mind. The Surangama Sutra sets forth and reveals this mind.

[Someone says: It is only called the true mind; has it yet other different names? The answer: In the teachings of the Buddhas and the teachings of the patriarchs the names established are not the same. And in the Buddhist teachings: the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra calls it the mind-ground, because it gives rise to all good; the Prajnaparamita Sutra names it bodhi, because it takes enlightenment as its essence; the Avatamsaka Sutra establishes it as the dharma-realm, because it interpenetrates and contains all; the Diamond Sutra names it the Tathagata, because it comes from nowhere; the Prajnaparamita Sutra calls it nirvana, because it is the refuge of all sages; the Golden Light Sutra names it suchness, because it is true and eternally unchanging; the Vimalakirti Sutra names it the dharma-body, because the reward-body and transformation-body rely on it; the Awakening of Faith names it true suchness, because it neither arises nor ceases; the Nirvana Sutra calls it the Buddha-nature, because it is the essence of the three bodies; the Perfect Enlightenment names it the all-holding dharani, because it pours forth merit; the Srimala Sutra names it the tathagata-garbha, because it hides, covers, and contains all; the Sutra of Definitive Meaning names it perfect enlightenment, because it shatters darkness and shines alone. Therefore the Chan Master Shou, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “One dharma, a thousand names; names are set up in accord with conditions.” They are complete in the many sutras, and cannot all be quoted.]

Someone asks: You have explained what the true mind is; has the true mind yet other names? The answer: The teachings and the Chan lineage give the true mind different names. In the teachings, the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra calls it the mind-ground, because it gives rise to all good; the Prajnaparamita Sutra names it bodhi, because it takes enlightenment as its essence; the Avatamsaka Sutra establishes it as the dharma-realm, because it interpenetrates and contains all; the Diamond Sutra names it the Tathagata, because it comes from nowhere; the Prajnaparamita Sutra calls it nirvana, because it is the refuge of all sages; the Golden Light Sutra names it suchness, because it is true and eternally unchanging; the Vimalakirti Sutra names it the dharma-body, because the reward-body and transformation-body rely on it; the Awakening of Faith names it true suchness, because it neither arises nor ceases; the Nirvana Sutra calls it the Buddha-nature, because it is the essence of the three bodies; the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment names it the all-holding dharani, because it pours forth merit; the Srimala Sutra names it the tathagata-garbha, because it hides, covers, and contains all; the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment again names it perfect enlightenment, because it shatters darkness and shines alone. Therefore the Great Master Yongming, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “One dharma has a thousand names; names are set up in accord with conditions.” The many names of the true mind in the teachings are all in the many sutras, and cannot one by one be fully quoted.

[Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra] Kumarajiva of the Yao Qin dynasty finally translated the tenth chapter, the Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts, of the Brahma Net Sutra, in two fascicles, entitled “The Brahma Net Sutra, Chapter Ten: The Bodhisattva Mind-Ground Precepts Spoken by Vairocana Buddha.” Later, the precepts spoken after the verses in the lower fascicle were extracted separately as one fascicle, for the convenience of recitation and upholding; the Tiantai master Zhiyi named it the Bodhisattva Precepts Sutra. [Prajnaparamita Sutra] The general name for the scriptures that set forth the profound and wondrous doctrine of prajnaparamita.

[Someone says: The Buddhist teachings are already known; what of the patriarchs’ teaching? The answer: Under the patriarchs’ gate, names and words are cut off; since no name is established, how could there be many more names? Yet in response to the stimulus of capacities, its names are likewise many.]

Someone asks: The many names of the true mind in the teachings are already known; then what names does the Chan lineage have? The answer: Under the patriarchs’ gate, names and words are cut off; since even a name is not established, how could there be many more names? Yet in response to the stimulus of capacities, the true mind has quite a few names.

[Sometimes it is called the self, because it is the nature of sentient beings; sometimes it is named the right eye, because it beholds all characteristics; sometimes it is named the wondrous mind, because it is empty and numinous, still and illuminating; sometimes it is named the master, because it has borne the burden from the first; sometimes it is called the bottomless bowl, because it makes its living wherever it is; sometimes it is called the stringless lute, because its melody comes forth in the present; sometimes it is named the inexhaustible lamp, because it shatters the deluded mind; sometimes it is named the rootless tree, because its root and stem are firm; sometimes it is called the sword of the hair-splitter, because it cuts off the roots of dust; sometimes it is named the land of the unconditioned, because the seas are calm and the rivers clear; sometimes it is named the Mani pearl, because it relieves the poor; sometimes it is named the boltiess lock, because it shuts the six senses; and further it is named the mud ox, the wooden horse, the mind-source, the mind-seal, the mind-mirror, the mind-moon, the mind-pearl.]

Sometimes it is called the self, because it is the nature of sentient beings; sometimes it is named the right eye, because it beholds all characteristics; sometimes it is named the wondrous mind, because it is empty and numinous, still and illuminating; sometimes it is named the master, because from the first it is the one that acts; sometimes it is called the bottomless bowl, because it lodges its living wherever it is; sometimes it is called the stringless lute, because its melody comes forth in the present; sometimes it is named the inexhaustible lamp, because it shatters the deluded mind; sometimes it is named the rootless tree, because its root and stem are firm; sometimes it is called the sword of the hair-splitter, because it cuts off the roots of dust; sometimes it is called the land of the unconditioned, because the seas are calm and the rivers clear; sometimes it is named the Mani pearl, because it relieves the poor; sometimes it is named the boltiess lock (a lock without a spring), because it shuts the six senses; and further it is named the mud ox, the wooden horse, the mind-source, the mind-seal, the mind-mirror, the mind-moon, the mind-pearl, and so on.
[The seas are calm and the rivers clear] The great sea has no waves, the Yellow River is clear. [Mani pearl] That is, the mani jewel, also named the wish-fulfilling pearl. [The spring of the “lock” (
xu
)] The reed-spring in a lock.

[These various different names cannot all be recorded. If one penetrates the true mind, all the names are understood; if one is benighted about this true mind, all the names become obstructions. Therefore, as to the true mind, one should be most careful.]

The various other names of the true mind cannot one by one be enumerated. If one penetrates the true mind, then as to all the names of the true mind one will understand that they are speaking of the true mind; if one is benighted about this true mind, then as to all the names of the true mind one will feel them obstructive, not knowing whether they speak of something else. Therefore, as to the various names of the true mind, one must judge by the context and discern them most carefully.

Here it must be explained that this one essence with different names, this one essence with many names appearing in the sutras and treatises, is for the sake of breaking students’ attachment to names and characteristics; the ancient Chan gate likewise customarily used this device of “one dharma, a thousand names; names set up in accord with conditions.” Yet one essence with many names is hard for modern people, educated from childhood in science, to accept. Some even reproach and challenge it on this account, holding it to be wrong, unscientific, and logically confused. For in science there is an unwritten rule: if a book or a paper is to use a technical term, it must first give a clear definition (except for terms familiar in textbooks), and from beginning to end it uses only that one term; if there is an exception, it must be noted. Therefore, when we study the sutras and treatises and meet this one essence with different names, one essence with many names, and even cases that cross and overlap, we should know that this is not the ancients’ logical confusion; they had their own intent. We ourselves must judge by the context what this or that name actually refers to, and accomplish “if one penetrates the true mind, all the names are understood,” so as to avoid misunderstanding.

blocks.text: 3. The Wondrous Essence of the True Mind

inline.s: [Someone says: The true mind’s name is already known; what of its essence? The answer: The Prajnaparamita Sutra of the Light-Emitting says: “Prajna has no characteristic of any kind, no characteristic of arising or ceasing.” The Awakening of Faith says: “The essence of true suchness itself: in all ordinary men, hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas, there is no increase or decrease. It is not born in the former limit, nor does it cease at the latter limit; ultimately it is eternal. From the very beginning its nature has of itself fulfilled all merit.”]

Someone asks: I already know the various names of the true mind; what then is the essence of the true mind? The answer: The Prajnaparamita Sutra of the Light-Emitting says: “Prajna has no characteristic of any kind, no characteristic of arising or ceasing.” The Awakening of Faith says: “The essence of true suchness itself: all ordinary men, hearers, solitary realizers, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas have no increase or decrease. It is not born in the former limit, nor does it cease at the latter limit; ultimately it is eternal. From the very beginning, the essence of the true mind of itself (by its own nature) fulfills all merit.”
[The former limit and the latter limit] The past is named the former limit; the future is named the latter limit.

[According to these sutras and treatises, the essence of the true mind transcends cause and effect, runs through past and present, establishes neither ordinary being nor sage, and has no opposites of any kind. Like great empty space it pervades all places; its wondrous essence is still and silent. It cuts off all idle discourse; it neither arises nor ceases, is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither moves nor shakes, and is clear and permanently abiding. It is called the master of former days, named the man on the far shore of Awesome Sound, and also named the self before the empty kalpa. With one equal mind, without the least flaw or film, all mountains, rivers, and the great earth, grasses, trees, and thickets, the myriad appearances in dense array, and all dharmas pure and defiled all come forth from within it.]

According to these sutras and treatises, the essence of the true mind transcends cause and effect, runs through past and present, establishes neither ordinary being nor sage, and has no opposites of any kind (no mutual opposition of this and that). Like great empty space it pervades all places; its wondrous essence is still and silent. It cuts off all idle discourse; it neither arises nor ceases, is neither existent nor nonexistent, neither moves nor shakes, and is clear and permanently abiding. It is called the master of former days, named the man on the far shore of Awesome Sound, and also named the self before the empty kalpa. With one equal mind (regarding all things equally), without the least flaw or film, all mountains, rivers, and the great earth, grasses, trees, and thickets, the myriad appearances in dense array, and all dharmas pure and defiled all come forth from within it.

[Idle discourse] Words that contain a playfulness and are unreal. [The far shore of Awesome Sound] Before the Buddha Awesome Sound King, or again before the appearance in the world of the Buddha Awesome Sound King. The Buddha Awesome Sound King is a Buddha who appeared in an extremely remote past age; the Chan groves borrowed this Buddha’s name to indicate a time in the past that is extremely remote. “The far shore (
pan)

] means that side. “The far shore of Awesome Sound” is a phrase the Chan groves commonly used to point students to their own original face, the same in meaning as “before one’s parents were born.” [The empty kalpa] One of the four kalpas, that is, after this world has been destroyed, during which there is only empty space. [The four kalpas] In one great kalpa there are the four intermediate kalpas of the kalpa of formation, the kalpa of dwelling, the kalpa of destruction, and the kalpa of emptiness, and each intermediate kalpa in turn has twenty small kalpas. What is called “formation” is the world being composed by the gathering of many conditions; “dwelling” is sentient beings abiding at rest, with plants and animals, with lands and borders, with history; “destruction” is the beginning of ruin: in the first nineteen small kalpas all plants and animals are destroyed, and in the last small kalpa the lands and worlds on which sentient beings rely are destroyed; “emptiness” is that when the destruction is complete, all alike become empty space. Thus the world unceasingly goes through formation, dwelling, destruction, and emptiness, cycling around without end. [Equal mind] An equal mind, without love and hate, taking and rejecting.

[Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good son, the supreme Dharma King has a great dharani gate named perfect enlightenment. From it flow forth all purity, true suchness, bodhi, nirvana, and the paramitas, teaching bodhisattvas.” Guifeng says: “As for the mind, it is empty and wondrous, subtle and pure, brightly luminous and numinously clear; it neither goes nor comes, and secretly penetrates the three times; it is neither middle nor outside, and thoroughly illumines the ten directions. It neither ceases nor arises: how could the four mountains harm it? It is apart from nature and apart from characteristics: how could the five colors blind it?” Therefore Yongming, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “As for this mind, all wonders and all spirits universally assemble in it, and it is the king of all dharmas; the three vehicles and the five natures secretly return to it, and it is the mother of a thousand sages. Alone honored, alone noble, without peer or equal, it is truly the source of the great Way, the essential truth of the Dharma.”]

Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good son, the Tathagata (the supreme Dharma King) has a great all-holding Dharma gate named perfect enlightenment. It ceaselessly flows forth purity, true suchness, bodhi, nirvana, and the paramitas, to teach bodhisattvas.” The Great Master Guifeng says: “As for the mind, it is empty and wondrous, subtle and pure, brightly luminous and numinously clear; it neither goes nor comes, and secretly penetrates the three times; it is neither middle nor outside, and thoroughly illumines the ten directions. It neither ceases nor arises: how could the four mountains (birth, old age, sickness, and death) harm it? It is apart from nature and apart from characteristics: how could the five colors (blue, yellow, red, white, and black) blind it?” Therefore the Great Master Yongming, in the Verses on Mind Only, says: “As for this mind, all wonders and all spirits universally assemble in it, and it is the king of all dharmas; the three vehicles and the five natures secretly return to it, and it is the mother of a thousand sages. Alone honored, alone noble, without peer or equal, it is truly the source of the great Way, the essential truth of the Dharma.”

[Empty and wondrous] Serene and still. [Brightly luminous] Bright and radiant. [The three times] Also named the three ages, that is, past, present, and future. [The four mountains] A simile for the four marks of birth, old age, sickness, and death. It means that birth, old age, sickness, and death have nowhere to be escaped, like four mountains closing in together. The Nirvana Sutra says: “There are four great mountains that come from the four directions, wishing to harm the people. The four great mountains are birth, old age, sickness, and death.” [The three vehicles] The vehicle of the hearers, the vehicle of the solitary realizers, and the vehicle of the bodhisattvas. [The five natures] The Faxiang school divided the faculties of all sentient beings into five kinds, called the five natures. First, those who have the undefiled seed by which the fruit of arhatship can be cultivated are named the definite nature of the hearers. Second, those who have the undefiled seed by which the fruit of the pratyekabuddha can be cultivated are named the definite nature of the solitary realizers. Third, those who have the undefiled seed by which the fruit of Buddhahood can be cultivated are named the definite nature of the bodhisattvas. Fourth, those who have two or three of the above kinds of undefiled seed, so that the stage they will realize in the future depends on conditions ripening and is not fixed as to which fruit they will realize, are named the indefinite nature. Fifth, those who do not have the undefiled seed of the above three vehicles but have the defiled seed by which the fruit of gods or men can be cultivated are named the natureless. [Without peer (
chou
)] There is none that can be compared with it.

[Believe it, and the bodhisattvas of the three times study together, for they study this mind; the Buddhas of the three times realize together, for they realize this mind; the whole canon of one treasury sets forth and reveals, for it reveals this mind; all sentient beings are deluded and confused, for they are deluded about this mind; all practitioners awaken, for they awaken to this mind; all the patriarchs transmit to one another, for they transmit this mind; the monks of the world under heaven call and visit, for they call and seek this mind.]

Believe as said above, and what the bodhisattvas of the three times study together is the study of this mind; what the Buddhas of the three times realize together is the realization of this mind; what the whole canon of one treasury sets forth and reveals is the revelation of this mind; all sentient beings are deluded and confused, for they are deluded about this mind; all practitioners awaken, for they awaken to this mind; all the patriarchs transmit to one another, for they transmit this mind; the monks of the world under heaven call and visit, for they call and seek this mind.
[For] A classical Chinese particle that introduces a statement.

[Penetrate this mind, and everywhere is the Way, and every thing fully manifests it; be deluded about this mind, and everywhere is inversion, and every thought is foolish madness. This essence is the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings; it is the root-source from which all worlds arise and develop. Therefore the World-Honored One was long silent on Vulture Peak, and Good Manifestation beneath the cliff forgot
(in ancient usage the same as “to die,” that is, to be silent)

words, Bodhidharma gazed at the wall at Shaoshi, and the layman held his tongue at Vaishali: all of them revealed the wondrous essence of this mind. Therefore one who has just entered the patriarchs’ gate must first recognize the essence of this mind.]

Penetrate this mind, and everywhere is the Way, and every thing fully manifests the wondrous principle; be deluded about this mind, and everywhere is inversion, and every thought is foolish and mad delusion. The essence of this mind is the Buddha-nature inherent in all sentient beings; it is the root-source from which all worlds arise and develop. Therefore the World-Honored One was long silent at the assembly on Vulture Peak, Subhuti sat in silence beneath the cliff, the patriarch Bodhidharma gazed at the wall at Shaolin Monastery, and the layman Vimalakirti held his tongue in the city of Vaishali: all of them used the wordless word to reveal the wondrous essence of this mind. Therefore one who has just entered the patriarchs’ gate must first recognize the essence of this mind.

[Everywhere is the Way] The state after awakening: mind and realm merge, inside and outside become one piece, and even eating and dressing, carrying water and gathering firewood, every movement and every act, every opening of the mouth and every closing of it, is a single matter undarkly merged with the “wondrous Way.” As is said, “Everywhere is the Way; every dharma is originally perfect.” [Vulture Peak] Gridhrakuta, Vulture Mountain, abbreviated Spirit Mountain, also translated as Mount Jijue; the mountain is named because its shape resembles a vulture and vultures were numerous on it. It lies northeast of Rajagriha, the capital of Magadha in Central India, and is the place where Śākyamuni Buddha taught the Dharma. [The World-Honored One was long silent on Vulture Peak] At the Lotus assembly on Vulture Peak (Gridhrakuta) the World-Honored One was long silent before revealing the meaning of the sutra; three times before this he only said: “Stop, stop; it need not be spoken. My Dharma is wondrous and hard to conceive.”]

[Good Manifestation] The translated name of Subhuti. [Good Manifestation forgot words beneath the cliff] Subhuti sat in silence (in still meditation) among the rocks, and the gods rained flowers in praise. The elder said: “You rain flowers in the sky and praise me; who then are you?” The answer: “I am Brahma.” The elder said: “What do you praise?” Brahma said: “I honor the venerable one for well expounding prajnaparamita.” The elder said: “I have never spoken a single word of prajna; what do you praise?” Brahma said: “The venerable one did not speak, and I did not hear. Not speaking and not hearing: this is truly expounding prajnaparamita.” And again the earth shook and flowers rained down. [Shaoshi] A separate peak of Mount Song. Emperor Xiaowen of Wei built the Shaolin Monastery there for the Chan Master Buddha, and it is the place where the First Patriarch Bodhidharma sat facing the wall for nine years. [Vaishali] The city of Vaishali, the dwelling place of the layman Vimalakirti. [The layman held his tongue at Vaishali] Vimalakirti once questioned the assembled bodhisattvas on the Dharma gate of non-duality, and they in succession set forth the meaning of non-duality in words; at the last Manjushri questioned Vimalakirti, and Vimalakirti held his tongue and silently did not answer, and Manjushri then sighed in admiration. For the Dharma gate of non-duality is beyond the reach of words and explanations, and so Vimalakirti’s single silence surpassed the words of all the bodhisattvas.
There was of old the koan of “Xiangyan strikes the bamboo”:

the Chan Master Xiangyan Zhixian was a man of Qingzhou. Weary of the vulgar he left his kin, and traveled the regions seeking the Way. In the time of Baizhang his nature and understanding were sharp and quick, yet he could not penetrate Chan. When
ji,
that is, when he had reached and come to
Baizhang passed into transformation
when he had come to the Chan Master Baizhang’s parinirvana

he went to study under Guishan. Guishan asked: “I have heard that in the place of your late master Baizhang you answered ten when asked one and answered a hundred when asked ten; this is your cleverness and sharp wit. Understanding and interpretation, consciousness and thought
this is

are the root of birth and death. Before your parents were born, try and say one phrase.” At this one question the master was utterly at a loss. He returned to his quarters and took up the texts he had read in former days, meaning to search from the beginning for a single phrase to answer with, yet in the end he could not find one. Then he sighed to himself: “A painted cake cannot fill the belly.” Again and again he begged Guishan to explain it to him. Guishan said: “If I explained it to you
if I were to explain it for you

you would curse me hereafter. What I say is mine, and in the end has nothing to do with you.” The master then burned all the texts he had read in former days, saying: “In this life I will not study the Buddha Dharma. I will be a long-traveling monk of gruel and rice, and spare my mind its labor.
He wept and took leave of Guishan. He went straight through to Nanyang, and seeing the traces of the National Teacher Zhong
the National Teacher Huizhong
he rested there. One day, as he was cutting
shan,
cutting grass
he happened to fling away a piece of tile, which struck a bamboo and made a sound, and he was suddenly awakened. Quickly
ju,
urgent

he returned, bathed, and burned incense, and from afar bowed in homage to Guishan, praising him: “The master’s great compassion exceeds that of my parents. Had he then explained it to me, how would there have been today’s matter?” And he had a verse, saying: “One strike, and knowing is forgotten; no more is cultivation needed. In every movement the ancient path is exalted
every movement manifests the ancient path of the sages: seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha
not falling into the trap of quiet stillness
not emptily guarding dead quietude
Everywhere without traces
the wondrous essence of the true mind
beyond sound and form its dignity
the dignity of the wondrous essence of the true mind surpasses sound and form
Those who have reached the Way in every quarter all speak of
all say
the supreme capacity.” When Guishan heard it, he said to Yangshan: “This one is thoroughly
greatly awakened

). Yangshan said: “This is the mind’s mechanism and consciousness, accomplished by writing. Wait until I myself have personally tested him.” Later Yangshan saw the master and said: “The master praises the junior brother for revealing the great matter. Try and say something.” The master recited his former verse. Yangshan said: “That was accomplished by memorizing former habits. If you have a true awakening, say something else.” The master made another verse: “Last year poor, it was not yet poverty; this year poor, then it is poverty. Last year poor, I still had ground to plant a needle (to stand a needle: ten thousand thoughts return to one); this year poor, there is not even a needle (there is not even ground to stand a needle: the one thought returns to nothing).” Yangshan said: “The Tathagata Chan, we grant, the junior brother understands. The patriarchs’ Chan, he has not dreamed of it.” The master had yet another verse: “I have one mechanism; a blink of the eye (a blink, the time of a blink) regards it (him). If a man does not understand, then (turning away) call him a novice monk.” Yangshan then reported to Guishan: “I am glad to say the junior brother Xian (Zhixian) understands the patriarchs’ Chan.” (from the Wudeng Yantong)

[Tathagata Chan] The Chan methods prevalent in the eastern land before Bodhidharma came from the west, such as breath-counting Chan, the five-gate Chan, and so on. Their characteristic is: relying on the teachings to cultivate contemplation, gathering the mind into concentration, and advocating liberation through meditative concentration.

[Patriarchs’ Chan] The Chan method transmitted by the patriarch Bodhidharma: not establishing words, a special transmission outside the teachings, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming a Buddha. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “It speaks only of seeing the nature; it does not discuss meditative concentration and liberation.” [A special transmission outside the teachings] The Chan school sets up no writings and establishes no words and phrases, but directly transmits the Buddha’s and the patriarchs’ mind-seal, which is called “a special transmission outside the teachings,” meaning a special transmission apart from the Tathagata’s verbal teachings. The Sutra of the Great Brahma King Asking the Buddha to Resolve Doubts says that the Brahma King came to Spirit Mountain and offered the Buddha a golden lotus flower, requesting the Buddha to speak the Dharma. The World-Honored One twirled the flower before the assembly and did not speak the Dharma, and for a time the millions of gods and men all failed to understand his meaning; only the Elder Kashyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: “I have the treasury of the correct Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvana, the mark of reality that is no-mark, the subtle and wondrous Dharma gate, which is not established in words and is a special transmission outside the teachings. I entrust it to Mahakashyapa.” This is the origin of the Chan school. Therefore the patriarchs’ Chan also originates from the Tathagata; it is only a special transmission outside the teachings. [The treasury of the correct Dharma eye] The Buddha’s mind-eye thoroughly beholds the correct Dharma, and is named the “correct Dharma eye”; being deep and wide and containing ten thousand virtues, it is called the “treasury.”

[I have one mechanism] The five aggregates of body and mind are constantly compared to a mechanical wooden man (a wooden figure driven by a mechanism). The “mechanism” in the phrase “I have one mechanism” is a simile for the mechanism (the self-nature) that drives the wooden man (the five aggregates of body and mind). The Treatise on the Perfection of Great Wisdom says: “There is no maker at all. Is this matter an illusion? Is it a mechanical wooden man, or a matter in a dream?” The Surangama Sutra says: “Though one sees the faculties moving, they must be drawn by one mechanism; when the mechanism is stilled and returns to silence, all illusions become without nature.” [A blink of the eye regards it] This is precisely the state the Fifth Patriarch Hongren spoke of in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch: “one who has seen the nature must see it at the word (as soon as it is spoken, he sees)”; and so Yangshan certified that Xiangyan understood the patriarchs’ Chan. [At the word] Beneath a single word; instantly. [Call him a novice monk] When the master (Yangshan) was a novice monk, a monk asked Shishuang: “What is the meaning of the patriarch’s coming from the west?” Shishuang said: “If a man in a well a thousand feet deep can get out without using an inch of rope, that man will answer you the meaning of the coming from the west.” The monk said: “Recently the monk Chang of Hunan has appeared in the world and likewise speaks east and west for people.” Shishuang called the novice monk: “Drag out this corpse.” The master afterwards asked Danyuan: “How can the man in the well get out?” Danyuan said: “Ha! Fool! Who is in the well?” The master went and asked Guishan. Guishan called: “Huiji (Yangshan’s name)!” The master responded. Guishan said: “He is out!” After the master had settled, he often brought up these former words and told the assembly: “I got my name at Danyuan’s place, and got my ground at Guishan’s place.” (From the Sayings of the Chan Master Huiji of Yangshan in Yuanzhou.)

[What is the meaning of the patriarch’s coming from the west?] The First Patriarch of Chan, Bodhidharma, came from the western heaven to this land to transmit the Dharma: what is its essential purport?

blocks.text: 4. The Wondrous Function of the True Mind

inline.s: [Someone says: The wondrous essence is already known; what is called its wondrous function? The answer: The ancients said: “When the wind moves, the mind shakes like a tree; when clouds arise, the nature stirs up dust. If one understands today’s matter, one is benighted as to the original man.” This is the wondrous function arising from the wondrous essence.]

Someone asks: The wondrous essence of the true mind is already known; what then is the wondrous function of the true mind? The answer: The ancients said: “When the wind of conditions moves, the mind shakes like a tree; when the clouds of obstruction arise, the nature stirs up dust like dust; if one takes the things around one as real and is turned by them, one loses the original man.” This is the wondrous function arising from the wondrous essence of the true mind.

This passage says that even what is done in delusion is the wondrous essence of the true mind at work, only that it is the perverse function of the true mind when deluded. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“The self-nature can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and is named the storehouse consciousness. If thinking arises, that is the turning consciousness, which produces the six consciousnesses, goes out through the six gates, and sees the six dusts; thus the eighteen realms all arise as functions of the self-nature. If the self-nature is perverse, it gives rise to eighteen perverse functions; if the self-nature is right, it gives rise to eighteen right functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if the function is good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature.”

(Translation: The self-nature (the true mind) can contain the ten thousand dharmas, and so is named the storehouse consciousness. If the self-nature gives rise to thinking, that is the turning consciousness, which produces the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). The six consciousnesses go out through the six gates (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind) and see the six dusts (form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharmas). Thus the eighteen realms (the six consciousnesses, the six gates, and the six dusts) are all the self-nature at work. If the self-nature is perverse, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen perverse functions; if the self-nature is right, these eighteen realms give rise to eighteen right functions. If the function is evil, it is the function of sentient beings; if good, it is the function of the Buddha. From what does the function come? It comes from the self-nature (the true mind).)

[The true mind’s wondrous essence is originally unmoving, quiet, true, and eternal. When the wondrous function appears upon the true essence, it is no hindrance to follow the stream and attain the wondrous. Therefore the patriarch’s verse says: “The mind follows the ten thousand conditions; where it turns, it is truly profound. Following the stream, one recognizes the nature; without joy and without sorrow
(without love and hate, taking and rejecting)

.” Therefore at all times, in all movement and action, going east and west, eating and dressing, picking up the spoon and handling the chopsticks, looking left and glancing right, it is all the wondrous function of the true mind appearing.]

The wondrous essence of the true mind is originally unmoving, quiet, true, and eternal. When the wondrous function appears upon the true essence, it is no hindrance to follow the stream and attain the wondrous. Therefore the patriarch’s verse says: “The mind follows the ten thousand conditions; where it turns, it is truly profound. Following the stream, one recognizes the nature; without joy and without sorrow (without love and hate, taking and rejecting).” Therefore at all times, in all movement and action, going east and west, eating and dressing, picking up the spoon and handling the chopsticks, looking left and glancing right, it is all the wondrous function of the true mind appearing.
This passage says that if one “follows the stream and recognizes the nature,” then all movement and action is the right function of the true mind when awake.
[The mind follows the ten thousand conditions; where it turns, it is truly profound] Knowing all dharmas without being moved by them. The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “
He well discerns the characteristics of all dharmas
(the characteristics of all dharmas)
yet in the foremost meaning
(the true characteristic of all dharmas)
he does not move.”
The Mahaparinirvana Sutra says

“All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is named the real, that is named the true characteristic, that is named the dharma-realm, named the ultimate wisdom, named the foremost meaning truth, named the foremost meaning emptiness.”

[The foremost meaning truth] The supreme, perfect, and ultimate truth. [Following the stream, one recognizes the nature] As time flows on, one always recognizes the nature of the characteristics of all dharmas that one meets —
“all characteristics are false and delusive”

(the Diamond Sutra). This is “meeting characteristics and returning to the nature”: deluded thoughts are originally still, the dusts of the senses are originally empty; empty and still without darkness, still and illuminating before one. In this way one is not bound and turned by the characteristics of the senses — following the stream, one attains the wondrous.

[Ordinary men are deluded and inverted: when dressing, they take it only as dressing; when eating, they take it only as eating; in all their affairs they merely follow characteristics, and so the true mind is in daily use and they do not notice it, is before their eyes and they do not know it. But one who recognizes the nature does not lose the true mind in movement and action.
