Therefore the patriarch says: “In the womb it is called the body; in the world it is called a man; in the eye it beholds, in the ear it hears, in the nose it smells fragrance, in the mouth it talks, in the hand it grasps, in the foot it runs. When it manifests everywhere it contains the sand-grain worlds; when it gathers in, it is held within a single mote of dust.... Those who know it take it as the Buddha-nature; those who do not call it the spirit.”]

Ordinary men are deluded and inverted: when dressing they take it only as dressing, when eating they take it only as eating, and all that they do merely follows characteristics (they do not “follow the stream and recognize the nature”); and so the true mind is in daily use and they do not notice it, and is before their eyes and they do not know it. But one who recognizes the nature does not lose the true mind in movement and action. Therefore the patriarch says: “The true mind in the womb is called the body; in the world it is called a man; in the eye it beholds, in the ear it hears, in the nose it distinguishes fragrance, in the tongue it talks, in the hand it grasps, in the foot it runs. When the true mind manifests everywhere, it contains worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges (describing how great the true mind is when it manifests everywhere); when the true mind gathers in, it can be held within a single mote of dust (describing how small the true mind is when it gathers in). Those who know it know this is the Buddha-nature; those who do not call it the spirit.”

[When it manifests everywhere it contains the sand-grain worlds, when it gathers in it is held within a single mote of dust] This speaks of the true mind being able to be great and able to be small. [Sand-grain worlds] Worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The sands of the Ganges are a figure for a number that is very, very many.

[Therefore Daowu danced with his tablet, Shigong drew his bow, Mimo raised his fork, Juzhi held up a finger, the one of Xinzhou struck the ground, and Yunyan showed the lion: none of them was other than revealing this great function. If in daily use one is not deluded, one is naturally free and unobstructed in every direction.]

Therefore Daowu danced with his tablet, Shigong drew his bow, Mimo raised his fork, Juzhi held up a finger, the one of Xinzhou struck the ground, and Yunyan showed the lion: none of them was other than revealing the wondrous function of the true mind. If in daily use one is not deluded and inverted, one is naturally free and unobstructed in every direction.

[Daowu danced with his tablet] A monk asked the monk Daowu: “What is the meaning of the patriarch’s coming from the west?” The master (Daowu) bowed with his slip (bamboo tablet), saying: “Yes.” [Tablet (
hu
)] The bamboo tablet held by ministers at court audiences in ancient times, used for noting matters.
[Juzhi raised a finger] The monk Juzhi (
zhī

), when he had just taken up residence in his hut, was visited by a nun named Shiji. She wore a bamboo hat, carried a staff, and circled the master three times, saying, “If you can say it, I will take off my hat.” She asked this three times, and each time the master had no reply, so the nun left. The master said, “The sun is getting late; why not stay for a while?” The nun said, “If you can say it, I will stay.” Again the master had no reply. After the nun had gone, the master sighed, “Though I have a man's body, I have no man's spirit. I would rather abandon this hut and travel about seeking good and wise teachers.” That night the mountain spirit told him, “There is no need to leave this place; a bodhisattva in flesh will soon come to teach the Dharma to the master.” After more than ten days, sure enough, the monk Tianlong arrived at the hut. The master at once came out to greet and bow to him and told him the whole matter. Tianlong raised one finger and showed it to him, and the master was instantly greatly enlightened. From then on, whenever a student came to ask about anything, the master would simply raise one finger and give no other exposition. There was a young boy who, whenever he saw people ask about anything, also raised his finger. People said to the master, “Master, the boy also understands the Dharma; whenever asked, he raises his finger just as you do.” One day the master concealed a knife in his sleeve and asked the boy, “I hear you understand the Dharma, is that so?” The boy said, “It is so.” The master said, “What is the Buddha?” The boy raised his finger, and the master cut it off with the knife. The boy cried out and ran away. The master called the boy; the boy turned his head. The master said, “What is the Buddha?” The boy raised his hand and, seeing no finger, was suddenly greatly enlightened. When the master was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, “I obtained the one-finger Chan of Tianlong, and in a whole life I did not use it up.” Having said this, he entered extinction. [Tipiao] Also written as tichang or tigang, meaning to raise up and sing the essentials. That is, the way the Chan grove takes up and sets forth the essentials of the school to students. Generally one sings out the essential words of the ancients, so it is also called niangu (picking out the old) or niannong (handling the old). This is because the purpose of the Chan school is a special transmission outside the teaching, not relying on written words; therefore, although one speaks the recorded sayings, one only points to the essentials of the school, and students who wish to understand this matter must diligently study and investigate. Other schools call this jiangshi (explaining) or jiangyi (expounding the meaning).
[The earth-striking monk of Xin (
xīn

) Prefecture] A monk of Xin Prefecture, after he had awakened under Master Mazu, hid his name. Whenever a student came to seek instruction, he would only strike the ground with a stick to show him. Everyone called him the earth-striking master. In “the earth-striking one of Xin Prefecture,” the “Xin Prefecture” is an honorific usage of old times in which a person is named by his place; here it stands for the earth-striking master. [Yunyan's lion] Chan Master Yaoshan asked Chan Master Yunyan, “I hear you are very good at dancing the lion, is that so?” Chan Master Yunyan said, “It is so.” Yaoshan said, “How many acts can you dance?” Yunyan said, “I can dance six acts.” Yaoshan said, “I too can dance the lion.” Yunyan said, “How many acts can you, Master, dance?” Yaoshan said, “I dance one act.” Yunyan said, “The one is the six, the six is the one.” After Yunyan had been awakened and realized his understanding, he once came to visit Chan Master Weishan. Weishan asked, “I hear that you danced the lion at Yaoshan's place, is that so?” Yunyan said, “It is so.” Weishan asked, “Do you dance continuously, or is there a time when you stop?” Yunyan said, “When I want to dance, I dance; when I want to stop, I stop.” Weishan asked, “When you stop, where is the lion?” Yunyan said, “Stop, stop!”

blocks.text: 5. Substance and Function, One and Different

inline.s: (Original title: The substance and function of the true mind, one and different)

[Someone asks: The substance and function of the true mind, I do not know whether they are one or different? Answer: In terms of characteristics they are not one; in terms of nature they are not different. Therefore this substance and function are neither one nor different.]

Question: The substance and function of the true mind, I do not know whether they are one or two? Answer: In terms of characteristics they are two; in terms of nature they are one. Therefore the substance and function of the true mind are neither one nor two.

[How do we know this is so? Let me try to discuss it: The wondrous substance is unmoving, cutting off all duality, apart from all characteristics; only one who has reached and realized the nature can fathom its principle. The wondrous function follows conditions, responding to all the many kinds, falsely establishing empty characteristics, seeming to have shape. By this having characteristics and being without characteristics, they are not one. Again, the function issues from the substance, so the function does not depart from the substance; the substance can put forth the function, so the substance does not depart from the function. By this principle of their not being separated, they are not different.]

How do we know that the substance and function of the true mind are neither one nor two? Let me now explain it for you: The wondrous substance of the true mind is unmoving, cut off from all duality, apart from all characteristics; none but one who has realized the nature and verified it can easily understand this principle. The wondrous function of the true mind follows conditions, responding to the many kinds, falsely establishing empty characteristics, seeming to have shape. By the substance being without characteristics and the function having characteristics, the substance and function of the true mind are not one. Again, the function issues from the substance, so the function does not depart from the substance; the substance can put forth the function, so the substance does not depart from the function. By this principle of the substance and characteristics not being separated, the substance and function of the true mind are not two.

[Just as water takes wetness as its substance, and because the substance is unmoving, the wave takes movement as its characteristic, arising because of the wind. The water's nature is unmoving while the wave's characteristic moves, so they are not one. Yet outside the waves there is no water, and outside the water there are no waves; their wetness is one, so they are not different. By analogy, the one and different of substance and function can be understood.]

For example, water takes its wet nature as its substance, and this substance is unmoving; the wave takes movement as its characteristic, arising because of the wind. The water's nature is unmoving while the wave's characteristic moves, so they are not one. Yet outside the waves there is no water, and outside the water there are no waves; their wetness is one and the same, so they are not two. As described above, the principle of the one and different of the substance and function of the true mind becomes clear.

blocks.text: 6. The True Mind in Delusion

inline.s: [Someone asks: The substance and function of the true mind are possessed by everyone; why is it that sages and ordinary people differ? Answer: The true mind of sages and ordinary people is originally the same. Ordinary people, with their deluded mind, grasp at objects, and losing their own pure nature, are cut off by this, so the true mind cannot appear before them. It is but like the shadow of a tree in the dark, or a spring underground, present yet unrecognized.]

Question: The substance and function of the true mind are possessed by everyone; how is it that sages and ordinary people are entirely different? Answer: The true mind of sages and ordinary people is originally the same. But ordinary people, with the deluded mind, cling to the dusty realms (the deluded mind grasping at objects), lose their own pure nature, and being cut off by this, the true mind cannot appear before them. At this time the true mind is like the shadow of a tree in the dark, or a spring underground, present but hidden and not appearing.

[Therefore the sutra says: “Good man, just as a pure mani jewel reflects the five colors, each appearing in accordance with the direction, the foolish see the mani jewel as truly having the five colors. Good man, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment appears in body and mind, responding to each class in its own way; the foolish say that the pure perfect enlightenment truly has such self-characteristics of body and mind. It is the same as well.”]

Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, just as a pure mani jewel reflects the five colors, each appearing in accordance with the direction, the foolish falsely see the mani jewel as truly having the five colors. Good man, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment appears in body and mind, responding to each class in its own way; the foolish erroneously take the pure perfect enlightenment as truly having such self-characteristics of body and mind. It is likewise.”

[The Zhao Treatise says: “Within heaven and earth, between the cosmos, there is a single jewel, hidden in the form-mountain.” This is the true mind wrapped in defilement. Again, Ci'en says: “The Dharma body is originally present, common to all the Buddhas. Ordinary people, covered by delusion, have it yet do not realize it; wrapped in afflictions, it receives the name of the tathagatagarbha.” Sir Pei says: “One who is roundly enlightened all day long yet never roundly enlightened is an ordinary person.” Therefore we know that although the true mind is in the midst of worldly toil, it is not stained by worldly toil; like a white jade cast into mud, its color does not change.]

The Zhao Treatise says: “Within heaven and earth (the cosmos), between the universe, there is a single jewel (the true mind), hidden in the form-mountain (secretly buried in the physical body).” This is the true mind wrapped in defilement. Again, Master Kuiji says: “The Dharma body is originally present, common to all the Buddhas of the three times. Yet ordinary people, covered by delusion, have it yet do not realize it; wrapped in afflictions, it receives the name of the tathagatagarbha.” Pei Xiu says: “One who is roundly enlightened all day long yet never roundly enlightened is an ordinary person.” Therefore we know that although the true mind is in the midst of worldly toil, it is not stained by worldly toil, just as a white jade cast into mud, its pure white color does not change.

[The Zhao Treatise] It is a collection of the treatises written by the monk Sengzhao (zhào) of the Later Qin, and the whole book is divided into five parts: the Essence of the Ancestral Teaching, the Treatise on the Non-Movement of Things, the Treatise on the Non-True Emptiness, the Treatise on Prajna as Non-Knowing, and the Treatise on the Unnameable Nirvana; at the end are appended Liu Yimin's letter of inquiry and the reply to Liu Yimin. Sengzhao was one of the most outstanding and influential disciples under Master Kumarajiva, and among the disciples the youngest and most talented. [Tathagatagarbha] The natural state of one's intrinsic nature is called the tathagatagarbha. (For details see
Mind, Intrinsic Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha

[Kuiji] The founding patriarch of the Consciousness-Only school. Because he lived in the Great Kindness and Compassion Monastery of the capital, he was called “Master Ci'en.” He was the only son of the early Tang meritorious minister Yuchi Gong, of an intelligent nature and a majestic physique. At seventeen he was commanded to go forth as a monk, becoming a high disciple of Master Xuanzang, studying Buddhist scriptures and treatises and Indian languages under him; at twenty-five he took part in translating the scriptures. In the fourth year of the Xianqing era of Emperor Gaozong (the year 159), when Master Xuanzang translated the treatise On the Completion of Consciousness-Only and other works, Kuiji alone served as the amanuensis, producing the ten scrolls of the On the Completion of Consciousness-Only, one scroll of the Verse of the Treatise on Discerning the Middle and the Extremes, three scrolls of the Treatise on Discerning the Middle and the Extremes, one scroll of the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only, one scroll of the Treatise on the Doctrines of the Different Schools, and three scrolls of the Treatise on the Elements of Body and Base of the Abhidharma. Thereafter Master Xuanzang further expounded to Kuiji Dignaga's Gate of Correct Reasoning and the Treatise on the Yogacara Ground and other treatises. Thus Kuiji penetrated the science of logic and the doctrines of the five natures, and produced vast commentaries, and so was called the master of a hundred commentaries.
Question: What is fundamental ignorance?

Answer: Fundamental ignorance (also called beginningless ignorance) is the first stirring of thought. Because of this single thought rising, the intrinsic nature (the true mind) turns from awareness into delusion, dark and obscured through the long night, not understanding the truth, and giving rise to all the various delusions and afflictions.
Question: “From one thought of non-awareness arise the three subtle marks; with characteristics as the condition grow the six coarse marks.” What does this mean?
Answer: This describes the process of the intrinsic nature passing from awareness into delusion and producing delusion
creating karma
and receiving its retribution. The “three subtle and six coarse marks” are the nine false marks of arising and ceasing, of transmigration
into delusion
illusorily
manifested
by
the intrinsic nature

: the mark of ignorance and karma, the mark of being able to see, the mark of characteristics (the mark of what is seen); the mark of intelligence, the mark of continuity, the mark of grasping, the mark of attaching to names, the mark of producing karma, and the mark of suffering bound by karma.

Of these, the first three arise from fundamental ignorance (“from one thought of non-awareness arise the three subtle marks”); their marks are subtle, so they are called the “three subtle marks.” The latter six grow from the characteristic being the condition (“with characteristics as the condition grow the six coarse marks”); their marks are coarse and manifest, so they are called the “six coarse marks.”
The process is
“The three subtle marks”: First, the mark of ignorance and karma. The mind's movement is karma, so
the unminding mind that moves (the first stirring of thought)
is called the mark of ignorance and karma. Second, the mark of being able to see. Depending upon the foregoing
“mark of ignorance and karma,”
the mind moving, it can see. Third, the mark of characteristics (the mark of what is seen). Depending upon the foregoing “mark of being able to see”
since it can see, characteristics falsely appear.
“The six coarse marks”: First, the mark of intelligence. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of characteristics”
falsely producing the activity of intelligence and discriminating favorable and unfavorable, beautiful and ugly, love and aversion. Second, the mark of continuity. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of intelligence”
discriminating the conditions of objects, thought after thought continuing. Third, the mark of grasping. Depending upon the foregoing “mark of continuity”
turning deeper upon the thoughts of continuity, giving rise to self and what is mine, forming the mark of grasping. Fourth, the mark of attaching to names. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of grasping”
and naming the various states, affairs, and things, forming concepts and language. Fifth, the mark of producing karma. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of attaching to names”
thinking and calculating, producing the various karma of body, speech, and mind. Sixth, the mark of suffering bound by karma. Depending upon the foregoing “mark of producing karma”,
bound by the karma of body, speech, and mind that is produced
it is bound
and experiences the bitter fruit of birth and death.

Question: Sentient beings are originally Buddhas; because of one thought of non-awareness they have ignorance and fall into being sentient beings. If one practices and attains buddhahood, could one again have a thought of non-awareness and ignorance, and fall back into being a sentient being?

Answer: No. Now, when we practice and attain buddhahood, it is precisely to eradicate beginningless ignorance. Therefore, after attaining buddhahood, one will not again have ignorance and fall into being a sentient being. This is like a person who, when he has not yet had smallpox, is a healthy person; having had smallpox, he becomes a sick person; after he recovers, he is again a healthy person and, possessing lifelong immunity, will never have smallpox again. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the bodhisattva Vajragarbha also asked this question: “Sentient beings of the ten directions originally accomplished the Buddha-way, and afterwards gave rise to ignorance. When will all the Tathagatas again produce all afflictions?” The World-Honored One answered: “Good man! It is like smelting a gold mine; the gold does not exist because of the smelting. Once it has become gold, it will not be turned back into ore.

The perfect enlightenment of the Tathagata is likewise.” (Translation: Good man! As in smelting and refining a gold mine, the gold does not exist because of the smelting; since it has already become pure gold, it will not again become ore.
The perfect enlightenment of the Tathagata is also like this, and does not reverse.)

blocks.text: 7. Stillling the Deluded Mind of the True Mind

inline.s: [Someone asks: The true mind dwelling in delusion, then one is an ordinary person; how can one come out of delusion and become a sage? Answer: The ancients say: “Where the deluded mind is nowhere, that is bodhi; birth and death and nirvana are originally equal.” The sutra says: “That sentient being, his illusory body being extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished; the illusory mind being extinguished, the illusory dust is also extinguished; the illusory dust being extinguished, the illusory extinction is also extinguished; the illusory extinction being extinguished, what is not illusory is not extinguished. It is like polishing a mirror; when the dust is gone, the brightness appears.”]

Question: The true mind dwelling in delusion, then one is an ordinary person; how can one come out of delusion and become a sage? Answer: The ancients say: “When there is no deluded mind, that is bodhi; birth and death and nirvana are originally equal.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “That sentient being (the one who practices the contemplation of extinguishing illusion), in his contemplation, his illusory body being extinguished, the illusory mind (the illusory consciousness) is extinguished; the illusory mind being extinguished, the illusory dust (the world) is extinguished; the illusory dust (the world) being extinguished, the contemplation that extinguishes illusion also is extinguished (the illusory extinction likewise extinguished; this is getting the fish and forgetting the trap, casting off layer after layer); the contemplation being extinguished, there remains only the pure perfect-enlightenment mind, not of the same as the illusory, which is not extinguished, like polishing a mirror; when the dust is gone, the brightness appears.”

[Bodhi] Translated into Chinese as “awakening,” it refers to the wisdom that can know the Dharma-nature, that is, the great wisdom that exhausts all afflictions. [Getting the fish and forgetting the trap (
quán

)] The trap, also written “quan,” is a bamboo implement for catching fish. It means that once the fish is caught, one forgets the implement. It is a metaphor for, once success is attained, forgetting what one relied upon; or, once the goal is reached, setting aside the means and method. [Birth and death and nirvana are originally equal] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Perfect enlightenment universally shines; quiescence and extinction are non-dual. Amid it, the hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas of inexpressible Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are like flowers in empty space, arising and ceasing in confusion. Neither identical with nor apart from, neither bound nor released, then one knows that sentient beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth and death and nirvana are like a dream of last night.” (For the commentary, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

[Yongjia also says: “The mind is the root, the dharmas are the dust; the two are like the traces upon a mirror. When the traces and dust are gone, the light appears; when mind and dharma are both forgotten, the nature is true.” This is coming out of delusion and becoming true.]

Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way also says: “The consciousness-mind is the six faculties (of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind); the various dharmas are the six objects (forms, sounds, scents, tastes, tangible objects, and mental objects). These two (the consciousness-mind and the dharmas) are like the traces upon the mirror (the mind-essence); when the traces and dust are gone the mirror's light appears, and when mind and dharma are both extinguished (the faculties and objects fall away) it becomes the state of the true mind.” This is what is meant by the true mind coming out of delusion and becoming true (the return from delusion to the state of awareness).

[When mind and dharma are both forgotten, the nature is true] With the consciousness-mind and the various dharmas both extinguished, one returns to the state of awareness of the true mind. In classical texts, “wang” is used for “wang” (to extinguish).
[Someone asks: Master Zhuang says: “The mind, when hot, scorches
(used for “scorched”)

like fire; when cold, congeals like ice; so swift that in the twinkling of an eye it again roams beyond the four seas; when still, deep and quiet; when moving, hanging aloft in the sky, this is only the human mind!” This is Master Zhuang first speaking of how the ordinary person's mind is hard to subdue. I do not know by what method the school treats the deluded mind? Answer: By the method of no-mind it treats the deluded mind.]

Question: Master Zhuang says: “The mind, in its fierceness, is hot like a blazing fire; in its decline, cold like a bitter frost; so swift that in the twinkling of an eye it can again wander beyond the four seas; when at rest, deep and serene; when moving, leaping up to the high heavens, I fear only the human mind can do this!” This is the late Master Zhuang first speaking of how the ordinary person's mind is so hard to subdue. I do not know by what method the school treats the deluded mind? Answer: By the method of no-mind one treats the deluded mind.

[The twinkling of an eye] The time of a single lowering and raising of the head. It describes an extremely short time. [Deluded mind] The true mind dwelling in a state of delusion (the true mind in delusion) is called the deluded mind.

[Someone asks: If a person has no mind, he is the same as plants and trees; the saying of no-mind, please give the expedient means. Answer: What I call no-mind does not mean being without the mind-essence, called no-mind. It is only that in the mind there is nothing, and this is called no-mind. For example, an empty bottle is called an empty bottle because there is nothing in the bottle, not because the bottle's substance does not exist. Therefore the patriarch says: “You have only to have no affairs in the mind, and no mind in the affairs; then naturally it is empty and spiritual, still and wondrous.” This is the purport of this mind. According to this, the point is to have no deluded mind, not to be without the wondrous function of the true mind.]

Question: If a person has no mind, he is the same as plants and trees; the saying of no-mind, please analyze it in detail for me. Answer: What I call no-mind does not mean that being without the mind-essence is called no-mind. It is only that in the mind there is nothing, and this is called no-mind. For example, when one speaks of an empty bottle, it is called an empty bottle because there is nothing in the bottle; it is not called an empty bottle because the bottle's substance does not exist. Therefore the patriarch says: “You have only to have no affairs in the mind, and no mind in the affairs; then the mind-essence naturally is empty and spiritual, still and wondrous.” This is the essential purport of stilling the deluded mind of the true mind. According to this, stilling the deluded mind of the true mind takes having no deluded mind as its essential purport; it does not mean being without the wondrous function of the true mind.

The Essentials of the Dharma of Mind-Transmission says: “Therefore, the student of the Way, only recognizing seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, and the functioning of action, if he empties out seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, then the path of the mind is cut off, and there is no place to enter; he has but to recognize the original mind at the place of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. Yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, nor does it depart from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. Only, do not form views upon seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing; do not move the thought upon them; do not seek the mind apart from them; and do not reject seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing to grasp the dharma. Neither identical with nor apart, neither abiding nor attached, free everywhere at will, there is nowhere that is not the way-place.”

It also says: “Therefore, the student of the Way, deluded about his own original mind, does not recognize it as the Buddha, and so seeks outside, engaging in the practice of functions, making progress by stages, toiling through countless kalpas, and never accomplishing the Way. It is preferable to be without mind in the present moment, with certainty knowing that all dharmas are originally without any possession and also without any attainment, without reliance and without abiding, without subject and without object, without moving a false thought, and then verify bodhi. When one verifies the Way, one verifies only the original-mind Buddha; the toil of kalpas is all empty cultivation. Like the warrior who obtains the jewel, he obtains only the original jewel on his forehead, having nothing to do with the effort of seeking outside.”

[The jewel on the forehead] Using the jewel on the forehead as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (the true mind) originally possessed by everyone. The Nirvana Sutra gives this parable: a warrior wrestling with another, their heads colliding, the diamond jewel between his brows sank into his skin, and a sore grew there. Later a good physician told him of it, and only then did he know the diamond jewel had entered his body. This is a metaphor for how all sentient beings, because covered by afflictions, do not know the Buddha-nature they originally possess; once they encounter a good and wise teacher, only then do they come to see the Buddha-nature they originally possess.
[From of old, the various masters' methods of practicing the no-mind work have each been different; now summarizing their great meaning, I briefly indicate ten kinds:]

The methods of practicing the no-mind work spoken of by the various patriarchs of the past, by category, are each different; now I will gather them together as ten kinds and briefly explain them as follows:

blocks.text: 1. Awareness and Stillling Delusion

inline.s: [The first is called awareness. It means that when doing the work, ordinarily one is without thought, guarding against the rising of thoughts. The moment a thought arises, one immediately breaks it with awareness. When the false thought is broken by awareness, the following thought does not arise. When the work is mature, this awareness-wisdom is also not needed, and both delusion and awareness are forgotten. This is called no-mind. Therefore the patriarch says: “Do not fear that thoughts arise; only fear that awareness is slow.” And a verse says: “Do not seek truth; only be still your views.” This is the work of stilling delusion.]

The first is awareness. When doing the work, ordinarily one is in the state of no-thought (ordinarily without thought), guarding against the rising of thoughts at all times. The moment a thought arises, one immediately breaks it with awareness; when the false thought is broken, the following thought does not arise. When the work is mature, this awareness-wisdom is also not needed, and both false thoughts and awareness are extinguished. This is called no-mind. Therefore the patriarch says: “Do not fear that thoughts arise; only fear that awareness is slow.” He also says: “You need not seek the true mind; only still the arising of thought (be still your views), and the true mind naturally appears.” This is the work of stilling false thoughts.

blocks.text: 2. Resting and Stillling Delusion

inline.s: [The second is called resting. It means that when doing the work, one thinks neither of good nor of evil; when a thought arises, one rests it; when a condition is met, one rests. The ancients say: “Go like a single bolt of white silk, go cold and forlorn; in the old temple, go like the incense burner.” When one reaches the point of cutting off all subtle activity and separation, free of discrimination, like a dullard or a blockhead, then there is a little corresponding. This is the work of resting the deluded mind.]

The second is called resting. When doing the work, one thinks neither of good nor of evil; when a thought arises, one rests it (does not continue it); when a condition is met, one rests (does not cling). The Chan Master Shishuang (Qingzhu of the Tang dynasty) says: “Go like a single bolt of white silk, go cold and forlorn; in the old temple, go like the incense burner.” Until one has extinguished the subtle rising of thought and freed oneself from all the false views of clinging discrimination, like a dullard or a blockhead, only then is there a little correspondence. This is the work of resting false thoughts.

[A single bolt of white silk] White silk: white silk cloth. Here the white silk is a metaphor for the mind-thought being pure and unmixed, the state of the ten thousand thoughts converging into one. “Go like a single bolt of white silk” means to take away even that single thought (the one returning to nothing), and enter the state of no-thought. [In the old temple, go like the incense burner] The incense burner of the old temple (the single wisp of incense-fire remaining in the old temple): a metaphor for the mind-thought being pure and unmixed, the state of the ten thousand thoughts converging into one. “Go like the old temple incense burner” (taking away even the single wisp of incense-fire remaining in the old temple) is also a metaphor for the one returning to nothing and entering the state of no-thought. [Subtle activity] Fine and small.

blocks.text: 3. Extinguishing the Mind and Preserving the Realm

inline.s: [Third, extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm. It means that when doing the work, all false thoughts are extinguished. Paying no regard to the external realm, one has only to still one's own mind. The false mind being already stilled, what harm is there in having a realm? This is the ancients' approach of seizing the person and not the realm. Hence there is the saying: “Everywhere there is fragrant grass; the whole city is without an old friend.” And the layman Pang says: “Only be without mind toward the ten thousand things; what harm that the ten thousand things surround you?” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm.]

Third, extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm. When doing the work, all false thoughts are extinguished. Paying no attention to the external realm, one has only to still one's own mind. Because the false mind is already stilled, what harm is there in a realm? This is the ancients' approach of seizing the mind and not the realm. Hence the verse says: “Everywhere there is fragrant grass (the realm); the whole city is without an old friend (the mind).” And the layman Pang says: “Only be without mind toward the ten thousand things; what harm that the ten thousand things perpetually surround you?” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm.

blocks.text: 4. Extinguishing the Realm and Preserving the Mind

inline.s: [Fourth, extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind. It means that when doing the work, one contemplates all the inner and outer realms entirely as empty and still, preserving only the single mind, standing alone and unique. Therefore the ancients say: “Not to be companion to the ten thousand dharmas, not to be counterpart to the various dusts.” If the mind attaches to the realm, the mind is precisely the false mind; now that there is no realm, how can there be falsehood? It is the true mind alone shining, unimpeded in the Way, which is the ancients' approach of seizing the realm and not the person. Hence the saying: “The flowers of the upper garden have fallen; the carriages and horses are still thronging.” And again: “Where are the three thousand swordsmen today? Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace.” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind.]

Fourth, extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind. When doing the work, one contemplates all the inner and outer realms completely as empty and still (“whatever has characteristics is all vain and false”), preserving only the single mind, standing alone and unique (not connecting with the inner and outer realms). Therefore the ancients say: “Not to be companion to the ten thousand dharmas, not to have any connection with the various dusts.” If the mind attaches to the realm, then the mind is the false mind; now that there is no realm, where could there be a false mind? This is the true mind alone shining, not impeding the Way, which is the ancients' approach of seizing the realm and not the mind. Hence the verse says: “The flowers of the upper garden (the imperial garden) have withered (extinguishing the realm); there are still many carriages and horses gathered (preserving the mind).” And again: “Where are the three thousand swordsmen today? Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace.” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind.
[The carriages and horses still thronging (
pián tián

)] There are still many carriages and horses gathered there. [The three thousand swordsmen] Describing the world in great disorder, the many heroes contending (three thousand swordsmen), planning to pacify the world. [Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace] Reckoning it over, only Master Zhuang was lofty, transcending the world and departing from the common (the mind not seizing the realm, the realm naturally extinguished), enjoying peace.
However, the allusion of “Where are the three thousand swordsmen today? Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace” comes from the Zhuangzi
Miscellaneous Chapters

On Swords: King Wen of Zhao was so fond of swordsmanship that he spent all day with swordsmen and neglected the government of the state. Swashbucklers surged in, more than three thousand in number. They competed day and night in swordsmanship, and every year over a hundred were killed or wounded. This went on for three years, the state's strength waned day by day, and the lords of the various states were all plotting how to attack Zhao. The crown prince was deeply worried and invited Master Zhuang to go and persuade him. Zhuang Zhou said to King Wen of Zhao: “There are three kinds of swords, namely the sword of the Son of Heaven, the sword of the feudal lords, and the sword of the common people. Now the Great King holds the position of one who wins the world, yet delights in the sword of the common people; I privately deeply despise this for the Great King, and hope the Great King will grasp the sword of the Son of Heaven.” So King Wen of Zhao reflected deeply, and for three months did not leave his palace gate to watch swordsmanship. The three thousand swordsmen, losing favor and ashamed and angry, would not live dishonorably, and all killed themselves at their lodgings.

blocks.text: 5. Extinguishing the Mind and Extinguishing the Realm

inline.s: [Fifth, extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm. It means that when doing the work, one first empties the external realm, then extinguishes the inner mind. Since both inner mind and outer realm are still, how after all can delusion exist? Hence Guanxi says: “In the ten directions there is no wall; on the four sides there is also no gate; naked, utterly bare.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing both person and realm. Hence the saying: “The clouds scatter and the water flows away; still and silent, heaven and earth are empty.” And again: “Neither the person nor the ox is seen; it is exactly the time of the bright moon.” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm.]

Fifth, extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm. When doing the work, one first empties the external realm, and then extinguishes the inner mind. Since both inner mind and outer realm are still, after all from whence can delusion come? Hence the Master Guanxi says: “In the ten directions there are no windows (walls); on the four sides there is also no gate; naked (utterly bare), utterly bare.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing both mind and realm. Hence the verse says: “The clouds scatter and the water flows away; still and silent, heaven and earth are empty.” And again: “Neither the person (the cowherd) nor the ox (the ox he tends) is seen; it is exactly the time of the bright moon (the true mind shining alone).” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm.

blocks.text: 6. Preserving the Realm and Preserving the Mind

inline.s: [Sixth, preserving the realm and preserving the mind. It means that when doing the work, the mind abides in the position of mind, the realm abides in the position of realm. Sometimes when mind and realm confront each other, then the mind does not seize the realm, and the realm does not approach the mind; each not reaching the other, naturally false thoughts do not arise, and there is no hindrance to the Way. Hence the sutra says: “This Dharma abides in the position of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are permanent.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing neither person nor realm. Hence the saying: “A single moon rises from the sea; how many families go upstairs?” And again: “Mountain flowers in thousands of blossoms; the wandering son does not know to return.” This is the work of extinguishing delusion by preserving the realm and preserving the mind.]

Sixth, preserving the realm and preserving the mind. When doing the work, the mind abides in the position of mind, the realm abides in the position of realm. When mind and realm confront each other, then the mind does not seize the realm and the realm does not enter the mind; each not reaching the other (the mind and realm unhook), naturally false thoughts do not arise, and there is no hindrance to the practice of the Way. Hence the Lotus Sutra says: “This Dharma abides in the position of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are permanent.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing neither mind nor realm. Hence the verse says: “A single moon rises from the sea; how many families go upstairs?” And again: “Mountain flowers in thousands of blossoms; the wandering son does not know to return.” This is the work of extinguishing delusion by preserving the realm and preserving the mind.

[Each not reaching the other] The mind not seizing the realm, the realm not entering the mind; this is the “mind like a wall” that the Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted to the Second Patriarch Huike. (For details see
The Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entrances and Four Practices

) [This Dharma abides in the position of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are permanent] This Dharma, that is, should abide in the position of Dharma (not entering the mind); thus the characteristics of the world are the permanent true reality, that is, in the apparent arising and ceasing (the characteristics of the world), one sees only the unborn (true reality). This is what is meant by: “When the whole world praises him, he does not thereby rejoice; when the whole world blames him, he does not thereby be dejected; he is fixed in the distinction between inner and outer, clear about the realm of honor and disgrace.” (See the Zhuangzi, Wandering in the void.) Translation: When the whole society praises him, he is not therefore glad; when the whole society blames him, he is not therefore dejected. He can determine the boundary between the inner mind and outer realm, and clearly know that such outer realms as honor and disgrace are but illusions. (The “quan” in the line, used for “huan,” means joy. For example, the Hanfeizi, the Eight Villainies, says: “To please his mind and make him offend against his lord.”) [A single moon rises from the sea; how many families go upstairs?] The bright moon rising over the eastern sea, this is a beautiful scene, yet how many people go upstairs to enjoy it? This too is a metaphor for the realm and the mind, each not reaching the other, mutually unconcerned. [Mountain flowers in thousands of blossoms; the wandering son does not know to return] The mountain flowers in full bloom are a beautiful scene, yet the wandering son does not therefore return home to enjoy them. This too is a metaphor for the realm and the mind, each not reaching the other, mutually unconcerned.
The characteristics of the world ever abide.” As the Zhaolun says:

The whirlwind topples the mountains, yet all is ever still; the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; the dust of the fields billows and blows, yet it does not move; the sun and moon traverse the sky, yet they do not go round.

” (Translation: a fierce wind blows down the mountains, yet all is ever still; the rivers race and pour, yet they do not flow; the dust billows and blows, yet it does not move; the sun and moon course through the sky, yet they neither rise nor set.)

In this passage, “the whirlwind topples the mountains,” “the rivers race and pour,” “the dust of the fields billows and blows,” and “the sun and moon traverse the sky” — these describe the appearance (the characteristics of the world)

. Yet when viewed from the true characteristic of all dharmas, the whirlwind, the rivers, the dust, and the sun and moon do not exist at all (originally not a single thing); where then could there be any toppling of mountains, racing and pouring, billowing and blowing, or traversing of the sky? Therefore it is said: ever still, not flowing, not moving, not going round. (For details see the article
The True Characteristic of All Dharmas
The Heart Sutra says:
“This is the empty characteristic of all dharmas: not arising, not ceasing; not defiled, not pure; not increasing, not decreasing.”
(For detailed annotation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra

[Whirlwind] Also named the vaivarta wind, translated as: great fierce wind. This is the great fierce wind of the time of the kalpa disasters. [Kalpa disasters] The three disasters of fire, water, and wind that arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction; these three disasters sweep away the entire world. [The whirlwind topples the mountains] The great fierce wind of the time of the kalpa disasters blows down Mount Sumeru.

[The dust of the fields] A figure for dust. This says that in the season of spring, when the yang energy stirs, one gazes far off at the dust over the marshes and wild grass, and it seems like galloping horses; hence it is called “the dust of the fields.”

blocks.text: 7. The Whole of Inside and Outside

inline.s: [7. The whole of inside and outside. This says that when doing the work, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, the inner body and the outer world, and all dharmas are of one substance with the true mind, clear and empty, luminous, without a hair’s breadth of difference; the worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are beaten into one piece — from what place then could the deluded mind arise? Therefore the Dharma Master Sengzhao said: “Heaven and earth are of one root with me; the ten thousand things are of one body with me.” This is the work of stilling delusion by the whole of inside and outside.]

7. The whole of inside and outside (inside and outside become wholly one body). When doing the work, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, the inner and outer body and mind and the world of instruments, and all dharmas are all the very substance of the true mind, clear and empty, luminous, without a hair’s breadth of difference. The worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are beaten into one piece; from what place then could the deluded mind arise? Therefore the Great Master Sengzhao said: “Heaven and earth are of one root with me; the ten thousand things are of one body with me.” This is the work of stilling delusion by the whole of inside and outside.

[The world of instruments] The world of vessels and things: the general name for the mountains, rivers, and great earth, houses, and all implements and useful objects. It is synonymous with “the world of instruments and things.” [Worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges] Worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. [The great world] A thousand small worlds make one “small chiliocosm”; a thousand small chiliocosms make one “middle chiliocosm”; a thousand middle chiliocosms make one “great chiliocosm.” Because there are three multiples of a thousand in this, the great world is also named “the great trichiliocosm.”

blocks.text: 8. The Whole Function of Inside and Outside

inline.s: [8. The whole of inside and outside in function. This says that when doing the work, one contemplates all the dharmas of the inner and outer body, mind, and world of instruments, and all movements and activities, as the wondrous function of the true mind. The moment any thought of the mind arises, it is the wondrous function appearing before one. Since all is the wondrous function, where can the deluded mind settle? Therefore Yongjia said: “The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya.” The Twelve Hour Song of Lord Baozhi says: “At dawn, the hour of the tiger: within the wild mechanism hides the person of the Way; sitting or lying, he does not know that originally this is the Way, and only busies himself in toil and suffering.” This is the work of stilling delusion by the whole of inside and outside in function.]

8. The whole of inside and outside in function. When doing the work, one contemplates all the dharmas of the inner and outer body, mind, and world of instruments, and all movements and activities, as the wondrous function of the true mind. The moment any thought of the mind arises, it is the wondrous function appearing before one. Since all is the wondrous function of the true mind, where can the deluded mind settle? Therefore Master Yongjia says in the Song of Realizing the Way: “The true nature of ignorance is the Buddha-nature; the illusory, empty body is the dharmakaya.” Lord Baozhi says in the Twelve Hour Song: “At dawn, the hour of the tiger: within the wild mechanism hides the person of the Way; sitting or lying, he does not know that originally this is the Way, and only busies himself in toil and suffering.” This is the work of stilling delusion by the whole of inside and outside in function.
[Dawn] Early morning. [The tiger] The hour of the tiger (from three to five in the morning). [At dawn, the hour of the tiger] This is the time when cultivators of the Way rise from bed.

blocks.text: 9. Substance Itself Is Function

inline.s: [9. Substance itself is function. This says that when doing the work, though one is secretly united with the true substance in a single flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a numinous clarity: this is substance itself being function. Within that numinous clarity there is hidden emptiness and stillness: this is function itself being substance. Therefore Yongjia said: “Clear and aware together with still and silent is right; clear and aware together with wandering thoughts is wrong; still and silent together with clear and aware is right; blank and silent together with still and silent is wrong.” Since within the still and silent there is no room for blankness, and within the clear and aware there is no use for scattered thoughts, how can any deluded mind arise? This is the work of stilling delusion by substance itself being function.]

9. Substance itself is function. When doing the work, though one is secretly united with the true substance in a single flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a numinous clarity: this is substance itself being function. Within that numinous clarity there is hidden emptiness and stillness: this is function itself being substance. Therefore the Great Master Yongjia said: “Clear and aware together with still and silent is right; clear and aware together with wandering thoughts is wrong; still and silent together with clear and aware is right; blank and silent together with still and silent is wrong.” Since within the still and silent there is no room for blankness, and within the clear and aware there is no use for scattered thoughts, how can any deluded mind arise? This is the work of stilling delusion by substance itself being function.
[Clear and aware (
xīng xīng
)] The mind clear and wakeful. [Blank] Dull and torpid.

blocks.text: 10. Passing Beyond Substance and Function

inline.s: [10. Passing beyond substance and function. This says that when doing the work, one does not distinguish inside from outside, nor does one discern east, west, south, and north; the four quarters and eight directions are taken as a single great gate of liberation. Perfectly round and complete, substance and function are not divided, without the least leak or seepage, the whole body beaten into one piece — from what place could the delusion arise? The ancients said: “The whole body without a seam or crack, above and below all one round mass.” This is the work of stilling delusion by passing beyond substance and function.]

10. Passing beyond substance and function. When doing the work, one does not distinguish inside from outside, nor does one discern east, west, south, and north; the four quarters and eight directions are taken as a single great gate of liberation. Perfectly round and complete, substance and function are not divided, without the least leak or seepage, the whole body beaten into one piece — from what place could the deluded mind arise? The ancients said: “The whole body without a seam or crack, above and below all one round mass.” This is the work of stilling delusion by passing beyond substance and function.
[Seam and crack (
xià
)] A gap. [Too (
tè
)] Excessively, overmuch. [The round mass (
luán
)] The appearance of roundness; it refers to the full moon.

[The ten methods of doing the work set out above need not all be used; one has only to accomplish the work of a single gate, and the delusion of itself ceases and the true mind at once appears. One should follow one’s own faculties and past habits, and whichever dharma one has formerly had a karmic connection with, that one should practice. This work is a merit without merit, not a merit of deliberate effort. This Dharma gate of resting the deluded mind is of the utmost importance, and so it has been spoken of at length
(that is)
and not because the text is verbose.]

Of the ten methods of doing the work set out above, one need not use them all. One has only to accomplish the work of a single gate, and the delusion of itself ceases and the true mind at once appears. Therefore, following one’s own faculties and past habits, whichever method one has formerly had a karmic connection with, that is the method one adopts. These ten kinds of work are a merit without merit, not a merit of deliberate effort. Because this Dharma gate of resting the deluded mind is of the utmost importance, it has been spoken of at length; so please do not find it long-winded.

blocks.text: 8. The True Mind’s Four Deportments

inline.s: [The four deportments] An abbreviation of the four dignified deportments. [The four dignified deportments] These are the rules that monks and nuns must observe; that is, they must be careful in the movements of daily life in order to preserve gravity and dignity. The four dignified deportments are: walking, standing (standing still), sitting, and lying down. One should walk like the wind, stand like a pine, sit like a bell, and lie like a bow.

[Someone says: The stilling of delusion was spoken of above, but I do not know whether it is practiced only in sitting, or whether walking, standing, and the rest are also included? The answer: The sutras and treatises mostly speak of practicing in sitting, because it is easily accomplished; but walking, standing, and the rest are likewise included, because with long practice one gradually becomes thoroughly familiar with it.]

Question: The stilling of delusion was spoken of above, but I do not know whether one can only cultivate it sitting in stillness, or whether one can also cultivate it in walking, standing, and lying down? Answer: The sutras and treatises mostly speak of cultivating it sitting in stillness, because such cultivation is easily accomplished; and when one has cultivated sitting in stillness for a long time and gradually become thoroughly familiar with it, one can then cultivate it in walking, standing, and lying down as well.

[The Awakening of Faith says: “If one practices stilling, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with the mind set straight, not relying on the breath, not relying on form or color, not relying on emptiness, not relying on earth, water, fire, and wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. All thoughts, as they arise, are at once removed, and the very thought of removing them is also dismissed. For all dharmas are originally without thought: thought after thought not arising, thought after thought not ceasing. Nor may one, after letting the mind follow external objects of thought, then use the mind to remove the mind. If the mind scatters, one should at once gather it back and dwell in right thought. As for this right thought, one should know that there is only mind, with no external objects; and even this mind has no self-characteristic, for thought after thought cannot be obtained.”]

The Awakening of Faith says: “If one practices stilling, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with the mind set straight, not relying on the breath (not regulating the breath), not relying on form or color, not relying on emptiness, not relying on earth, water, fire, and wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. All thoughts, as they arise, are at once removed, and the very thought of removing them is also dismissed. For all dharmas are originally without thought: thought after thought not arising, thought after thought not ceasing. Nor may one, after letting the mind follow external objects of thought, then use the mind to remove the mind. If the mind scatters, one should at once gather it back and dwell in right thought. As for this right thought, one should know that all is only mind, with no external objects; and even this mind has no self-characteristic, because thought after thought cannot be obtained.

[Practicing stilling] Doing the work of stilling deluded thoughts. [Seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing] The general name for the consciousness-mind’s contact with external objects. The function of eye-consciousness is “seeing,” the function of ear-consciousness is “hearing,” the function of the three consciousnesses of nose, tongue, and body is “perceiving,” and the function of the mind-consciousness (the sixth consciousness) is “knowing.” [All thoughts, as they arise, are at once removed, and the very thought of removing them is also dismissed] “All thoughts, as they arise, are at once removed”: this is the work of bringing ten thousand thoughts to one. “And the very thought of removing them is also dismissed”: this is the work of bringing the one to nothing. [Nor may one, after letting the mind follow external objects of thought, then use the mind to remove the mind] For to “use the mind to remove the mind” in this way is to remove delusion with delusion and to follow delusion in its turning. This is a point that requires particular attention when doing the work of stilling.

[“If one rises from sitting and, in going and coming, advancing and stopping, has things to do, one should at all times recollect skillful means and observe in accord with conditions. With long practice one becomes thoroughly familiar, and one’s mind attains stability. Because the mind is stable, it gradually becomes keen and sharp, and one is able to enter, in accord with conditions, the samadhi of true suchness, deeply subduing the afflictions; faith grows, and one quickly attains non-retrogression. Only those who are doubtful, who do not believe and who slander, who have heavy karmic obstructions, or who are proud and indolent are excluded. Such people as these cannot enter it.” From this we may conclude that it also pervades the four deportments.]

If one rises from the seat, goes out and comes in, advances and stops, and has actions to perform, one should at all times use skillful means and observe in accord with conditions; and if the mind scatters, one should at once gather it back and dwell in right thought. When one practices thus for long and becomes thoroughly familiar, deluded thoughts do not arise (one’s mind attains stability). Because deluded thoughts do not arise (because the mind is stable), the power of concentration gradually becomes ever keener and sharper, and one is able to enter, in accord with conditions, the samadhi of true suchness, deeply subduing the afflictions; faith grows, and one quickly attains non-retrogression. Only the doubtful, those who do not believe and who slander, those with heavy karmic obstructions, and the proud and indolent are excluded. As for the samadhi of true suchness, such people as these cannot enter it.” According to this passage of instruction from the Awakening of Faith, the cultivation of stilling delusion by the true mind can be carried on in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

[The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “First, in reliance on the Tathagata’s samatha practice, firmly uphold the precepts, settle among the assembly of disciples, and sit in stillness in a quiet room.” This is the initial practice. Yongjia says: “Walking too is Chan, sitting too is Chan; in speech and in silence, in movement and in stillness, the substance is ever at peace.” From this we may conclude that it likewise pervades the four deportments.]

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “(Desiring the Tathagata’s pure perfect enlightenment of the mind, one should be of right thought and far removed from all illusions.) One should first cultivate stilling (first, in reliance on the Tathagata’s samatha practice); for this one must firmly uphold the precepts, settle among the assembly of disciples, and then sit in stillness in a quiet room and cultivate.” This speaks of the earliest stage of cultivating stilling, in which one must sit in stillness and cultivate. The Great Master Yongjia says: “Walking too is Chan, sitting too is Chan; in speech and in silence, in movement and in stillness, the substance is ever at peace.” According to this passage of instruction, the cultivation of stilling delusion by the true mind can be carried on in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

[Samatha] Translated into Chinese as “stilling.” [Settle among the assembly of disciples] To dwell in harmony with one’s disciples and the great assembly. [Sit in stillness] To sit silently in meditation.

[To sum up the power of the work: if one cannot still the mind even in sitting, how much less can one enter the Way in walking, standing, and the rest? But one who has used the work until thoroughly familiar cannot be startled into rising even should a thousand sages arise, and pays no heed even should ten thousand demons and spirits surround him — how much less could he fail to do the work while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down? Suppose a man harbors hatred for another: through walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, through eating and drinking and all his movements, he cannot forget it at any time; and one who desires and loves another is likewise so. Moreover, hatred and love are affairs of the deluded mind, and can yet be harbored within the deluded mind; now the doing of the work is a matter of no-mind, so why doubt that it cannot be constantly present in the four deportments? I fear only that one does not believe and does not do it; but if one does it and believes, then the Way in the midst of the deportments will certainly not be lost.]

To sum up: if one’s power in the work cannot still the mind even in sitting, how much less can one enter the Way in walking, standing, and lying down? But one who has used the work of stilling delusion by the true mind until thoroughly familiar cannot be startled into rising even should a thousand sages come, and pays no heed even should ten thousand demons and spirits surround him — how could he be unable to do the work while walking, standing, or lying down? Suppose a man harbors hatred for someone: through walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, through eating and drinking and all his movements, he cannot forget it at any time; and one who loves and takes delight in someone is likewise so, through walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, through eating and drinking and all his movements, unable to forget it at any time. Moreover, hatred and love are affairs of the deluded mind, and can yet be harbored within the deluded mind as it walks, stands, sits, and lies down; now the doing of the work is a matter of no-mind, so why doubt that the work cannot be constantly present before one while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down? I fear only that one does not believe and does not do it; but if one believes and does it, then the work of stilling delusion in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down will certainly not be lost.

blocks.text: 9. Where the True Mind Dwells

inline.s: [Someone says: When the deluded mind is stilled the true mind appears. But where now are the substance and function of the true mind? The answer: The wondrous substance of the true mind pervades all places. Yongjia said: “Never leaving the very spot, it is ever serene and still; seek it and you will know that it cannot be seen.” The sutra says: “Because of the nature of empty space, because it is ever unmoving, because in the Tathagata-store there is no arising and ceasing.” The great Fayan said: “Everywhere is the road to bodhi; every heading is the forest of merit.” This is where the substance is.]

The questioner asks: When the deluded mind is stilled the true mind appears. But where now are the substance and function of the true mind? The answer: The wondrous substance of the true mind pervades all places. The great Master Yongjia said: “(The true mind) never leaves the very spot, ever serene and still; seek it and you will know that it (the true mind) cannot be seen.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Because of the nature of empty space, because it is ever unmoving, because in the Tathagata-store there is no arising and ceasing.” The great Chan Master Fayan (Master Wenyi) said: “Everywhere is the road to bodhi; every heading is the forest of merit.” These all speak of where the wondrous substance of the true mind dwells.

[The wondrous function of the true mind appears in response to stimulus, like an echo answering a sound. Fadeng said: “From then to now it should not fall; clearly it is before the eyes. A wisp of cloud rises in the evening valley; a lone crane descends from the distant sky.” Thus Huayan of the Wei Prefecture said: “The Buddha Dharma is in daily use, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in drinking tea and eating rice, in the mutual exchange of words. Yet in what one does and does, when the mind is stirred to a single thought, it is no longer so.” From this we know that the substance pervades all places and can everywhere give rise to function; but because the presence and absence of conditions is unfixed, the wondrous function too is unfixed, though it is not that there is no wondrous function. Those who cultivate the mind, wishing to enter the sea of the unconditioned and ferry across birth and death, must not be deluded about where the substance and function of the true mind dwell.]

As for the wondrous function of the true mind, it appears in response to stimulus, like a mountain valley echoing a sound. The Chan Master Fadeng said: “From then to now it should not fall; clearly it is before the eyes. A wisp of cloud rises in the evening valley; a lone crane descends from the distant sky.” Thus the old Huayan of the Wei Prefecture, in the Pointing at the Moon Record, said: “The Buddha Dharma is in daily use, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in drinking tea and eating rice, in the mutual exchange of words. Yet in what one does and does, the moment the mind is stirred to a single thought, it is no longer so.” From this we know that the wondrous substance of the true mind pervades all places and can everywhere give rise to function; but because the presence and absence of conditions is unfixed, the wondrous function is likewise unfixed, though it is not that there is no wondrous function. Those who cultivate the mind, wishing to enter the sea of the unconditioned and ferry across birth and death, must not be deluded about where the substance and function of the true mind dwell.

blocks.text: 10. The True Mind Transcends Birth and Death

inline.s: [Someone says: I have heard that one who has seen the nature leaves birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old were see-the-nature people, and they all had birth and death; now I see that people in the world who cultivate the Way also have the matter of birth and death. How can it be said that one leaves birth and death?]

Someone asks: I have heard that one who has seen the nature leaves birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old were see-the-nature people, and they all had birth and death; now I see that people in the world who cultivate the Way also have birth and death. How can it be said that one “leaves birth and death”?

[One who has seen the nature leaves birth and death] The statement “one who has seen the nature leaves birth and death” is not accurate; what is meant is: one who has destroyed the attachment to self (for example, an arhat) leaves birth and death. [Attachment to self] Also called attachment to a person, that is, deludedly grasping body and mind as a self. [Leaving birth and death] This does not mean that the present body will not die, but that after the end of this lifespan (the death of the body), the consciousness will not go on to be reborn, and so there will be no more death.
For example, one who has realized the fruit of arhatship: when this lifespan ends, the consciousness will not go on to be reborn, but abides in nirvana.

Another example: once a reciter of the Buddha s name is reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, one has the diamond indestructible body of the Tathagata, forever free of old age, sickness, all suffering, and death, right up to Buddhahood. [Nirvana] The realm of liberation and unconditioned-ness free of birth and death and of affliction.
[It is said: Birth and death originally do not exist; they are delusively taken to exist. It is like one with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky
(flowers)

. Or one without the disease says: there are no flowers in the sky. The sick one does not believe it. When the eye disease is gone the sky-flowers destroy themselves, and only then does he believe the flowers are nonexistent. Even while the flowers have not yet ceased, they are also empty; but the sick man delusively grasps them as flowers, not that they really exist in substance.]
Answer: Birth and death originally do not exist; they are only delusively counted as existent. It is like a man with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky (
the sky-flowers
). One without eye-disease says to him: there are no flowers in the sky. The sick man does not believe it. When his eye-disease is cured, the sky-flowers he sees
in the sky
naturally vanish, and only then does he believe there are no flowers in the sky. In the final analysis, the sky-flowers
in the sky
were never extinguished (because they had never arisen
at all
, how could one speak of their extinction?), for the sky-flowers
in the sky
do not exist; this is nothing but the diseased man s delusion, thinking there are flowers there; they are not really existent.

[Birth and death originally do not exist; they are delusively taken to exist] Birth and death are an affair of the dream of transmigration, and originally do not exist. Yet the ordinary man delusively grasps body and mind as a self, and so when this lifespan ends he goes again to take rebirth and has another body. Where there is birth there must be death; if in this life one continues to delusively grasp body and mind as self, then after death one must go again to take rebirth and have yet another body. Thus birth and death revolve without end. Cultivation is to cut off this attachment to self, this delusively grasping body and mind as a self. Once the attachment to self is cut off, when this lifespan ends the consciousness will not go on to be reborn, and so there will be no more death.

[It is like one who delusively takes birth and death as existent; or one without birth and death tells him: originally there is no birth and death. When one day that person s delusion ceases, birth and death destroy themselves, and only then does he know that birth and death originally do not exist. Even while birth and death have not yet ceased, they are likewise not really existent, because birth and death are delusively taken to exist.]

It is the same with one who is deluded in the dream of transmigration, delusively taking birth and death as existent. When an awakened person (one without birth and death) tells them that originally there is no birth and death, they absolutely will not believe it. But if one day they awaken (the delusive attachment ceases), then birth and death destroy themselves (they leave birth and death), and only then do they know that birth and death originally do not exist. Only while the delusive attachment has not yet ceased is birth and death likewise not really existent; and this is nothing but the delusive attachment (as with eye-disease) giving rise to birth and death (delusively seeing the sky-flowers).
[The awakened person] The Certificate of the Way says:
“In the dream there are clearly the six destinies; after awakening it is utterly empty, without the great chiliocosm.”

Thus, when the arhat s deluding karma of birth and death is exhausted, he no longer receives a future existence (he no longer receives a body in a future life). So after their passing into nirvana there is no more birth and death.

[The sutra says: “Good son, all sentient beings from the beginningless past have had all manner of inverted views, like a deluded man who confuses the four directions, delusively taking the four great elements as the self-characteristics of the body and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects as the self-characteristics of the mind, just as the diseased eye sees flowers in the sky. Even as the mass of sky-flowers vanishes into empty space, one cannot say that there is a definite place of their extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, in that which is unarisen, delusively see arising and ceasing; therefore they are said to turn in the wheel of birth and death.”]
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment
says: All sentient beings, from
the beginningless past, in all
manner of inverted views, take
the illusory as real, just
as a person who has
lost his direction mistakes south
for north and east for
west; in the same way
they delusively take the body
formed of the four great
elements of earth, water, fire,
and wind as the self-characteristics
of the body, and the
thoughts arising from the six
roots contacting the six sense-objects
as the self-characteristics of the
mind. This is like
a diseased eye seeing
flowers, delusively seeing flowers
in the sky. And
further, when the diseased
eye is healed, the
many sky-flowers vanish into
empty space; at that
time one cannot say
they have a definite
place of extinction. Why?
Because they are illusory,
and have no place
of arising, since they
never arose, how could
there be a place
of arising? All sentient
beings, in the unarisen,
delusively see arising and
ceasing; this delusory seeing
of arising and ceasing
is what is called
turning in the wheel
of birth and death.
The four great elements: all physical matter in the world is composed of the four elements of earth,
water, fire, and wind, and so they are called great, the great earth, great water, great fire,
and great wind. Earth has hardness as its nature, water wetness, fire warmth, and wind movement. The
shadow-images of the six sense-objects: that is, thoughts. When the six roots contact the six sense-objects, all
manner of thoughts arise, and these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, so they are called the
shadow-images of the six sense-objects, the phantom images that appear when the six roots contact the six
sense-objects. Sky-flowers: that is, flowers in the sky; hua in ancient usage is the same as flower.

[Based on this scripture passage, one may be certain that having realized the perfect enlightenment of the true mind, one understands that there is originally no birth and death. Now knowing that there is no birth and death, yet being unable to escape birth and death — that is because the practice is still insufficient.]

Based on this scripture passage, being certain that one has realized the perfect enlightenment of the true mind, one will understand that there is originally no birth and death. Those who now know that there is no birth and death yet cannot escape it — that is simply because their practice is still insufficient!

[Being certain of the realization of the true mind of perfect enlightenment, that there is originally no birth and death] Once one is certain of having realized the true mind of perfect enlightenment, one understands that there is originally no birth and death. Therefore, for one who has realized the true mind of perfect enlightenment, the birth and death of the six destinies is indeed an illusion; and if the delusive attachment
(grasping body and mind as self — attachment to self)

ceases, then after their passing into nirvana the self-nature (consciousness) will not go into the six destinies to take rebirth, and so leave birth and death. To understand that there is no birth and death is to cut off delusion as to views; for the delusive attachment to cease is to cut off delusion as to thought. Therefore to escape birth and death one must cut off both delusion as to views and delusion as to thought. [Delusion as to views and delusion as to thought] Delusion as to views and delusion as to thought. Delusion as to views is the confusion and error of the ordinary man in the sphere of views, such as the five perverse views of the view of self, the view of extremes, the perverse view, the view of holding to views, and the view of holding to precepts.
